analyses.title: The Battalion of Six, the Ice That Got Drunk, and the Bait Plan
analyses.subtitle: I was in the room. This is not a recap. This is what the paper actually proves.
analyses.filed: 1 Aethel, 922 BF (Feyward clock) — after I walked out of that corridor
analyses.summary: The night did not fail because the wood was strong; it failed because the house already had a government, and the government is the Revel. Four rooms of fighting changed nothing. One rolled sheet from the eater changed everything. I am filing the argument, not the fight.
analyses.thesis:
I sat at that table. I heard the heir say the dwarf way, and Hjumpik name six people at a cold breakfast, and one of those names exactly once — I am not printing it until I hear it twice. I put ice into a tree that drank it like water. Then a house guard ran up the stair with a paper from the thing eating the house, and everybody moved.

The session filing tells you who cut what, so I will not. My reading is simpler and worse: **command was a costume, the Revel was the office, and the bait plan was written after the whistle.** Four rooms of killing changed nothing about who the house reports to; one rolled sheet from the eater did, and the house obeyed it like a drill it had practiced.

sections.heading: Nobody Signed the Battalion
sections.sourceAnchor: a commission nobody signed
sections.body:
Look at the commission before you look at the mound: six names on the back of a barrel tally, one struck through, signed by nobody — the way a drowning man writes himself a rope. *WAH! Six names on the back of a barrel tally. I have seen better paperwork attached to a cheese.* That is not a unit. That is a list a frightened heir needed to exist so he could stop drowning at a map table.

Hjumpik took it anyway, and I watched him take it, and both halves of that sentence deserve ink: it was courage, because somebody had to become the shape of the hole, and it was the whole problem, because **we treated a blank as authority because somebody needed us to.** A blank never once said stop.

The house already had officers. They were downstairs refusing reinforcements because their job is to guard him, which is what officers say when they have one instruction and no permission to think. A signed sheet could have moved them. A barrel tally could not, and six people held a corridor the house had swords enough to hold twice over.

sections.heading: I Heard the Sixth Name
sections.sourceAnchor: I heard it once
sections.body:
Do not write that the archive missed a name. I was standing in the cold hall when they were given — Randall, Brad, Timmy, Hank, Wyatt — and the hall was cold enough to see your own breath, with the kind of acoustics where a voice goes up into the beams and comes back thin, so the one after Randall said his name and the name did not survive its own echo. I heard it. I am waiting for the second hearing because this house burns first-hearings.

That is me being careful, and the care is also evidence: **the battalion was assembled faster than the paper could follow.** A unit you cannot name twice you also cannot bury, pay, or court-martial; the gap in my notebook is the size of the hole the unsigned sheet left.

sections.heading: The House Fights Itself First
sections.sourceAnchor: both strokes into Hank
sections.body:
Timmy's first useful action of the night was two strokes into Hank — steel into a man's shoulder, in the dark, at arm's length — both of them home, both of them ours. A sprite later did the same job to a sprite; on the lane, an expedition arrow found their own best blade — cold iron in warm shoulders, three times over. *WAH. Two strokes, both landing, both on our own man. The sound of it is still in my back teeth.* Three ledgers of damage before the wood had earned one.

I will not call it accident, because accident says the wood was messy and luck was thin, and the record says something colder: **the standing order lasted four minutes.** Six strangers with no shared drill do what frightened people do — swing at the nearest moving shape — and sometimes the shape is Hank.

If you only read the session, you will think the shrub was the first engagement. The first engagement was Timmy.

sections.heading: The Tree Was Thirsty. That Is the Finding.
sections.sourceAnchor: ice lance the length of a hallway
sections.body:
I named three options with their costs, with cold already gathering in my fingers. Then I threw the ice, and it flew the way I throw when I am showing off — enormous, accurate, hallway-long — and the tree drank it in under a second, the way a sponge takes a spill. *WAH! Hallway-long, dead accurate, and swallowed without so much as a hiss. I have never been so well aimed and so useless in the same second.*

The filing will make that a joke. It is not a joke: **matter that size vanishing into a plant is a statement about what the Revel is made of,** and the strike did not so much as slow the thing down.

I did not wound a tree. I fed a mouth. I said that in the wahbook. I am saying it here with my name on it.

sections.heading: The Only Document That Moved the House
sections.sourceAnchor: Order of the Revel
sections.body:
Four engagements. One corridor held and handed back. One kitchen barricaded. One dwarf still arguing about command when the house guard came up the stair two at a time, boots loud on the wood, with a rolled sheet in his fist and paper's particular advantage over argument: it can be obeyed by people who were never asked for an opinion.

*You civilians. We are evacuating. Order of the Revel.*

The fairies moved — no debate, no heir, no battalion — in the order you would use in a drill. **The eater issued the fire drill, and the house obeyed.**

I have the paper. Read the last line: signed for the Revel, by the Revel's own office, which means the thing digesting the house keeps an office, and the office issues safety instructions. If you only remember one exhibit from this night, remember that one.

sections.heading: The Tally Named Something We Did Not
sections.sourceAnchor: the Ravenous Host
sections.body:
Seventeen turns in the reading room, dust off the shelves and light through one high window: satyrs, sprites, a goblin with a staff, the Oracle twice into a shrub, one sprite archer who spent the whole engagement doing nothing and thereby survived it — *WAH. Seventeen turns, and the most dangerous thing in the room turned out to be the handwriting.* And then, in the tally's own hand, the line I keep returning to: the Ravenous Host.

I was in that room with a book about wine and a chestnut. I can describe every person I can point at, and I cannot classify that mark — a thing busy enough to lead the count, and thin enough that nobody in the room, me included, can point at it now.

**A name that appears once on a combat ledger and nowhere else is not flavor. It is a hole.** The investigation already opened a lead. Do not close it with a joke.

sections.heading: The Plan Arrived After the Damage
sections.sourceAnchor: Can't go wrong
sections.body:
Hjumpik's bait plan is a real sentence — let them come in, run the bait, gang up — with one load-bearing clause humming under it like a cracked beam you can feel through the floorboards: *can't go wrong.*

I am filing this as analysis, not mockery. The man had already lost the corridor once and needed the table to have a next page, and a plan written at that hour is what it is: **not a strategy that produced the night, but a strategy the night produced.** The wood was already through the wall. The Revel had already issued the only order anyone obeyed. The plan spent the most fragile thing in the room — one runner's body — and called the spending free.

analyses.verdict:
My verdict: the battalion existed as six bodies and one unsigned sheet, and it deserves remembering at that resolution. The fights were real. The command dispute was real — I said it, he told me to write it in the wahbook, I wrote it. None of that is the center of the night.

The center is the evacuation order. A house being eaten accepted safety instructions from the eater, on paper, at once; and until somebody is willing to be the person who stops the music, every other plan is interior decorating in a burning house.

Recommendations. Treat the Revel office as a government, not a monster description. Keep the sixth name off the page until the second hearing. Do not let the Ravenous Host become a punchline. And do not add my ice to the win column.

I fed it.

rolls.failure: Blocked, honestly: one lance is not a diet study. I know what I saw. I will not pretend I know the chemistry.

analyses.title: The Restricted City and the Opened Gate
analyses.subtitle: The archivist argues with a gate that believed a guildmaster
analyses.filed: 5 Aethel, 1040 BF — after the extraction, Material clock
analyses.summary: The Junction is not a city; it is a sign that wants to be one. Embercap proved the sign can be talked past. Toadette proved the shack is not a house. And the winch — the only door that ever mattered — was already on their side of the brick.
analyses.thesis:
I was not on that wall. What I have instead is a missing rat, a rust shack, a crayfish five feet long, and a medic who blessed people from a bear's back and went out cold twice — the kind of afternoon that looks, on paper, like a campaign, and reads, once you sit with it, like a door problem that Loyalists keep solving with bodies.

My reading is simple and I am signing it: **the restricted city is a costume, the guildmaster is a password, and the winch is the only honest object in the filing.**

Embercap's lie worked because the gate wanted a procedure more than it wanted Bowser. Toadette's pause worked because she still remembers what a guildhouse is for. Dewdrop is the invoice. And the rat — the only scout I trust on this page — did not come back.

I like this squad. That is my bias, filed here so you can discount it while I fail to. I will not let liking them turn a shack into a victory parade.

sections.heading: The Sign Wanted a Procedure
sections.sourceAnchor: Halt. Restricted city. Bowser Bros only.
sections.body:
I have seen real Bowser paper — stamped, countersigned, afraid of its own chain of command — and this was never it. This is a gate that borrowed a famous name so it would not have to invent a reason. *WAH! Real Bowser paper is afraid of itself. This was a plank with confidence.*

Watch the exchange, because it takes three moves. Embercap asked for an exception; the sign does not contain exceptions. He named a guildmaster; the sign does not contain a guildmaster either. And the crew opened anyway — a groan with rust in it, the sound of a latch giving to procedure rather than force. That is not a forged pass. That is a posting that missed having work.

I prefer the reading that these Bros have not seen Bowser in a while. The competing one is worse: they have, and they still take guild gossip as a hall pass. Under either reading the four of them walked in because the costume wanted to be worn.

I would have lied too. I am not proud of that, but I have sat behind that kind of paper and I know the relief of being handed a script; what still needles me, audits later, is everyone on that wall treating the sign as an opponent when it had already confessed to being a costume.

Cross-file: Bramblehaven taught this same plume that a town can be taken by force. The Junction taught him a town can be faked by a sash. I would rather fight the first one. I keep getting the second.

sections.heading: A Manor Is a Word You Point At
sections.sourceAnchor: If the guildmaster is sleeping anywhere, he would be sleeping in a guildhouse.
sections.body:
Toadette said the only adult sentence in the street. A guildmaster hosts. Hosts need a hall. A rust shack with a rag in the window is not a hall; it is a dare, its roofline sagging toward the alley, rust bleeding down the boards, like a man reconsidering his story.

The Goomba said poor town, and it was the only defense the shack had. Poverty is real — I have lived in worse rooms than that shack, and I still knew they were rooms. I resent how often one gets used to excuse the other.

She waited. The street did not like it, because stopping to disbelieve a manor is embarrassing in a way walking into a shack never is, and most squads choose the shack. That pause is the whole infiltration. She embarrassed the street instead.

I am not calling her a genius. I am calling her a person who still believes buildings mean things. Keep her. The next lie will be prettier.

If I had been there I would have made a joke about the rag in the window. That is my vice. Her pause did more than my joke would have, and I am putting that on the record so I cannot pretend otherwise later.

sections.heading: The Only Scout Who Told the Truth
sections.sourceAnchor: She should not have sent a rat to do reconnaissance. The rat had not come back.
sections.body:
Everyone wants the crayfish to be the picture. I want the empty lip of the pipe — cold iron, wet brick underfoot — where the steam comes up smelling of old metal and something is missing that should be small and alive and back by now.

*WAH. Everybody watched the enormous thing with the claws. The evidence was the small warm thing that did not come back.* A missing animal is not cute. A missing animal is a map that ended. Toadette sat on that fact instead of sending a second rat, and sitting on a fact in front of an army — quiet, packed, watching the back of her head — is the first correct command decision in this file.

I do not know what ate it, and I will not print a first hearing. Pipes eat things. Towns eat things. A Magikoopa who will not stay in one place eats things. The lead is already open in the investigation. Do not close it with a joke.

I used to send people I did not like to look around corners. I am not better than her. I am louder.

sections.heading: Five Feet Is a Decision, Not a Costume
sections.sourceAnchor: The honest measurement will call five feet.
sections.body:
I wanted a dragon. I always want a dragon — that is my problem and I am filing it, because a bias you admit to the page is a bias the page can correct for.

What the wall got was a crayfish you could trip over — wet shell, cold air, five feet of it clattering on the brick. She used it the way a good piton gets used — not admired, weighted: she held one Koopa on those ladders until the job was done, then swung a brick with a claw already dull from missing, and the claw learned manners from the brick. That is not a mural. That is a captain staying on a problem.

Scale is a Loyalist temptation. Bramblehaven taught the faction that size can be policy; this wall taught them, in the same handwriting, that size can also be a brick to the face.

If she had gone bigger, the ladders would have become a joke and Dewdrop would still have been bleeding on them. I prefer the five feet. I am annoyed that I prefer it.

sections.heading: The Door Was Always a Machine
sections.sourceAnchor: Embercap found the winch that pulls the gates, and started hauling.
sections.body:
Lay it out in order. They talked through a gate; the talk closed; they climbed; and then, with the fight still eating the ladders and a Goomba's death fresh on the brick under him, *WAH! While everyone else was solving the fight, one Toad went and solved the door.* Embercap moved the ladder, found the winch, and hauled — chain, rust, the gate yawning open for the one argument nobody had tried on it all afternoon: a hand.

That is the article. Not the Goomba. Not the murderer speech. The winch.

If the next crossing starts with another guildmaster, I will throw the plume myself. The inside of that gate is chain and leverage, and it does not care whose sash you borrowed to stand in front of it.

I keep thinking about how many Loyalist plans are speeches. This one ended when someone shut up and pulled.

Recommendation, again, because I do not trust anyone to scroll: next time you see a Bowser Bros sign, look for the chain. The chain does not care who you claim to represent.

sections.heading: Dewdrop Is Not a Method
sections.sourceAnchor: She folded around it the way a body folds when the afternoon has already used her once.
sections.body:
Speared on the climb. Up. Blessing from a moving back. Down. Dragged through a winch-door. Speared, lifted, bleeding, blessing other people from the back of a moving bear with his own hands shaking. Read it as a receipt, not a rescue: the ladders billed one medic twice, and the billing only stopped because the winch made a door where the ladders were. That is not toughness. That is a bill.

I will not merge her with the other Dewdrop in the ledger. This one is the scribe who will not stay down; the faction page already spent the other one. Two names can share a sound. They cannot share a spine.

If this squad keeps using ladders as a plan, file the next medic before the next lie. I like her. That is why I am being rude.

sections.heading: I Am Still Not Splitting the Bear
sections.sourceAnchor: The bear — the tally's word, Big R's body
sections.body:
A big warm animal with a man on its back, breathing hard in the cold. The wall called him Black Bear. The after-action called him ANCHOR. I call him Big R, and until somebody says the second name twice I am keeping one person in this filing, *WAH! One body, one bear, two names, and a tally that would happily march both of them.* Because names are how tallies grow extra soldiers and I will not sign a growth I cannot verify.

He boosted Embercap. He missed. He fell to a blast. He stood. He took a spear and five gold off a corpse, because that is what a siege does when the door finally works. He carried Dewdrop. He waited.

Waiting is the line. Everyone wants the first kill; what the captain needed, with the wounded out and the crayfish still coming, was a door that still had a person standing in it.

If a second hearing splits him, I will print the split. Until then I will not invent a second heavy to make the tally look tidy.

analyses.verdict:
My verdict: they did not enter a city. They entered a story a gate tells itself, found a shack, and left by a machine.

Keep the lie off the next briefing. Keep the rat off the next briefing. Keep Dewdrop off the next ladder until someone else can bleed first. If you must go back, go for the winch, not the guildmaster.

The Magikoopa is still somewhere that is not a shack. The sign is still up. And the army is still at the pipes, watching the back of a captain who now knows what five feet of crayfish costs her.

That is enough spice. The rest is people wanting a mural.

analyses.title: The Scorncrow Skirmish: Deforestation, Garlic Weapons, and Wario's Stalled Motorbike
analyses.subtitle: The archivist argues the squad paid full price for a draw, and the grove kept the receipts
analyses.filed: After 30 Harvestide, 1040 BF — night
analyses.summary: The squad held the field and lost the ledger. My reading is that the elixir, the anthem, the giant's bellow, and Wario's stalled motorbike are one entry filed four times: the party bought its edge loudly, spent it in a single engagement, and carried home one sentence of intelligence. The Scorncrow was not beaten that night. It declined to attend.
analyses.thesis:
I was not on this field, which is the correct seat from which to bill it. What I hold is the filing, the receipts, and one sentence from a tree. My argument is that the Scorncrow Skirmish was not a battle at all. It was an auction of attention, and the grove won it by waiting.

Read the ledger the way I had to. The squad purchased its edge at Wario's counter — a bottle with a warning label — and drank it on instruction before anyone had so much as seen the enemy. It announced itself three separate times: a giant bellowing that he was a monster, a company of Toads singing their arrival across the dark, and a motorbike that roared exactly one entrance's worth of fun before a bush repossessed it. It spent its consumables against a thing that laughed at the pinning shot and left through the air. And what came back? A swing nobody sat in, bats nobody counted, feathers nobody collected, and a declaration — *"Sadly, I am not a monster"* — that nobody could ask a follow-up question of, because nothing was holding the declarant in place.

I am not calling the squad incompetent, and I want that on the record before anybody quotes me at a hearing. Markop's arithmetic at the vanguard was correct and lonely. Remi's report from the giant's shoulder was the only honest sentence filed from the entire field, which the event itself has the grace to admit. Eager's shot was perfect; it was simply an answer to a question nobody had asked yet. My grievance is narrower and worse than incompetence: the party keeps paying retail for information it could have at wholesale, because nothing in its method requires the enemy to spend anything back.

The grove took payment in noise, garlic, and elixir, and gave back one sentence. That is not a defeat. It is an invoice. WAH.

sections.heading: The Plan Was a Purchase, and the Purchase Was Most of the Plan
sections.sourceAnchor: Markop formed his plan around a single bottle: a Wario-branded elixir, warning label prominently displayed, distributed to the squad with instructions to drink it.
sections.body:
The most thoroughly verified document on that entire field was a warning label — small print on a glass bottle, read twice in bad light by a man who had already decided to drink it. Think about what that means. *WAH! The single best-audited object on that field was a bottle, and the audit was performed by the man drinking it.* Not the scouting report — there was none. Not the enemy assessment — the filing's own intelligence on the Scorncrow's nature begins and ends with the thing's exit line. The one paper everybody consulted, trusted, and acted upon before contact was the sticker on Wario's bottle, and the event records, with evident astonishment, that for once in Wario's catalog the label was telling the truth.

They drank it, the filing says, because the alternative was facing the Scorncrow sober. That is a joke, and jokes are where plans confess. Command by consumable is not inherently a sin — armies buy edges constantly, and a quartermaster who refuses to purchase advantage is a pacifist with paperwork. But look at the shape of the night: the elixir was distributed on instruction, consumed on faith, and the aftermath files its absence in the same breath as the garlic and the stalled motorbike. The squad's superiority had a supply chain and one item of stock. A plan whose center is a purchase is a plan that expires at the exact moment it works, because that is the moment the purchase is consumed.

The competing reading deserves its paragraph. Markop read the label. He verified the claim before betting the squad on it, which is more verification than most adventurers perform on their own weapons — his own warhammer arrived pre-seasoned in garlic, a doctrine at least consistent with itself. Buying an edge is logistics, and logistics is half of war.

My recommendation is smaller than my complaint: next purchase, record what the bottle actually did, against whom, for how long. The label promised bonuses against fey, undead, and other monsters — a category the enemy later declined, in writing, to belong to. Until the party files what the elixir bought them, the second bottle is a habit wearing the uniform of a decision.

sections.heading: Three Fanfares, Zero Scouting
sections.sourceAnchor: "Fi fi foe — I am a monster," he bellowed across the grove; the Toads marched in singing; Wario roared in on a motorbike that stalled in the branches.
sections.body:
Count the announcements. *WAH! Three separate noises, each one a letter of introduction posted to every crow in the grove.* One: a giant announcing himself to the entire grove in the tone of a man who has decided volume is the only remaining introduction. Two: a marching column of Toads singing their arrival, boots on cold ground, an anthem carrying through the dark. Three: a motorbike engine, a roar of promised fun, and then the bushes declining to let the rider anywhere else. Three separate signatures broadcast at a patient enemy, and not one pair of eyes sent ahead to learn anything before the singing started.

I concede the anthem before anybody makes me. The filing itself notes the song was the only thing in the grove that sounded like it knew where it was going, and marching songs do real work — they move a column, they keep frightened people facing forward, they turn a walk toward a monster into something a person can survive emotionally. Morale is a legitimate supply. But morale that announces your position is a loan against surprise, and the interest rate on that loan is set by the enemy. The Scorncrow's entire method that night was patience. Volume is a weapon only against an opponent that cares about being seen, and the filing records precisely nothing to suggest this one needed to see them. It needed them to arrive tired, loud, and out of elixir. They obliged on all three counts.

And then there is the jurisdictional dispute, which I have read four times and enjoyed more each time. Wario, mid-battle, claiming the chumps were under his command and not the giant's — a territorial filing over the ownership of a scarecrow, contested by bellow. The grove ruled on it immediately: the motorbike stalled before it had travelled the length of its own entrance. Whatever court the bushes keep, it has jurisdiction over Wario, and its judgments are enforced in branches.

The recommendation is one decision, made in advance: arrive quietly, or arrive so overwhelmingly that the noise is itself the weapon. A singing column escorting a stalled motorbike is neither, and against a patient grove it is a down payment on somebody's funeral.

sections.heading: Archie Accounted for Himself, and Nobody Audited the Books
sections.sourceAnchor: "I thought you were dead," Markop said. "We have a situation going on," Archie replied.
sections.body:
There is a missing wizard in this file, and the file lets him summarize his own absence. He walks back onto the field in one piece, with dust on his coat and both hands empty, and nobody asks him a single question. Long story short, stuff happened, lots of drastic turns, and umm, here and there — *WAH. Stuff happened. Drastic turns. Here and there. I have prised more detail out of a locked drawer.* A man caught at the worst possible moment, with grit in his beard and his boots wet to the ankle, offering a summary of nothing, deferring the full story to a time that never arrives within the filing. The party's response was to accept the return, heal him a little, and put him to work behind a wall of borrowed fire. An unaudited reappearance, processed as personnel.

I want to be fair, because the fair reading is strong: mid-battle is the wrong time for an audit. Triage is not negligence. A wizard who is breathing and casting is worth more than a wizard who is interrogated, and Markop did press him — the record shows the questions being asked, about the tree, about the pulling, about where he had been. The questions were asked. It is the answers that were deferred, and deferral is how absences compound. The archive now holds a man whose whereabouts across an entire missing interval are filed under "stuff," countersigned by nobody, dated never.

Here is my confession, since self-implication is worth more than superiority: I would have accepted it too, and for worse reasons. When somebody we have already mourned walks back in mid-crisis, relief audits nothing. The paperwork feels like sacrilege at exactly the moment it is most needed. That is why the audit has to be scheduled rather than felt — the filing itself says right now is not the time, which is an admission that a time exists and is owed.

And the audit protects *him*, which is the part nobody files. The day Archie's stuff happened turns out to hide something the grove cares about, the party will want dates, witnesses, and a direction of travel, and they will want them from the night the memory was fresh. Maybe there is nothing to find and the story is merely embarrassing. Fine. Embarrassment is cheap to file and cheaper to read. An empty file costs a paragraph; an unanswered one can cost a squad.

sections.heading: "It's Called Deforestation": The Noun Did the Targeting
sections.sourceAnchor: "Yes. It's an evil tree." / "You can. Uproot it, leave the ground — it's called deforestation."
sections.body:
Archie names his method like a man reading off a permit, with the smell of scorched bark already on his coat. The filing describes the flat confidence of somebody who has recently attempted exactly that and is not finished attempting it, *WAH! He said it like a noun on a form. It was a fire in a grove full of people.* And I believe the filing, because only a man mid-attempt talks that way about it. Uproot it, leave the ground — it's called deforestation. He is correct about the vocabulary. The method is real, too: against something rooted, removing the root is simply correct, and the event's own assessment concedes he was not wrong about the method, only about the enemy.

My argument is that the error happened one step earlier than the method, in the naming. "It's an evil tree" is not an observation; it is a filing decision. Once the thing is filed as a tree, uprooting follows logically, the flank toward a trunk follows logically, the pinning shot at the feet follows logically — and so does the surprise when the answer to all of it leaves through the air in smoke and crow-feathers. The vanish is the counter-filing. A tree cannot decline to be a tree. Whatever stood in that grove accepting garlic and arrows as the price of a good joke, it filed its own taxonomy on the way out — *I am not a monster* — which is a denial, not a description, and the party should notice that the only entity willing to classify the Scorncrow that night was the Scorncrow.

Category is targeting. Taxonomy is tactics. I keep a shelf of plans that failed at the noun, and I am not proud of how many of them are mine; the difference between Archie and me is that my trees usually stay pulled.

So the recommendation is a writing exercise, which I know is the least popular kind. Before the next engagement, one sentence — what the Scorncrow *is*, in terms the whole squad signs. If the sentence cannot be written, that inability is the intelligence, and it should send somebody back to the Tree of Woe file before it sends anybody else into the grove.

sections.heading: The Swing Was a Second Offer, and the Refusal Was the Only Negotiation the Party Won
sections.sourceAnchor: The Scorncrow answered Remi's arrival by summoning a playground swing into the grass beside her. "You want to swing again?" the tree asked.
sections.body:
The most loaded word in the entire filing is "again." *WAH! One word, and it turns a piece of playground furniture into a witness with a memory.* A swing stands in the grass beside a girl on a dark field — two ropes, one plank, still faintly moving, and the tree that put it there asks whether she wants to swing *again* — the ropes creaking in cold air over dead grass, which means the instrument has a history, and the history is already in this archive. The Tree of Woe engagement records the same offer in the same family of shapes: a swing descending on thick ropes, an invitation to sit, and Remi's own recovered notes noticing the spike on the top and the noose on the back. Two filings, one invitation, one addressee. The thing in the grove has a memory, and it repeats its instruments.

Remi declined. Oh. Okay, she said, and shot the tree instead, on Markop's warning that the swing would impale her — a warning worth its own line of praise, because it was specific, timely, and obeyed, which is more than most battlefield communications manage. The refusal was correct. But look at what the refusal actually *is*, beyond survival: it is data. The Scorncrow tested whether she remembered the last swing, and she did. The filing records the swing as a hazard. It is closer to an interview — the enemy asking the party a question about its appetites, in furniture.

The competing reading: "again" is reflex, the way anyone says *back for more?* to a returning face, and I grant that a taunt is not always a repertoire. But taunts are also repetition, and repetition can be mapped. A thing with a finite repertoire can be anticipated; a thing with infinite improvisation cannot. The archive cannot currently say which the Scorncrow is, and it could have started to say so that night, because for the first time both offers were on file within a week of each other.

Recommendation: keep a page for the instruments this thing reuses — swings, laughs, exits. Every repeated invitation narrows what it will try next, and patience, which is the only weapon it has shown, cannot dodge a pattern.

sections.heading: A Perfect Shot Is Not a Question
sections.sourceAnchor: Eager loosed a single shot — a critical hit, aimed deliberately at the Scorncrow's feet in an attempt to pin the thing down. The Scorncrow laughed.
sections.body:
This was the squad's finest moment and its clearest evidence of the gap between marksmanship and method. Steady hands, cold barrel, dust and bark in the air. The shot was perfect. *WAH! A hand, an eye, and a barrel put exactly where they were meant to be — and nobody in the grove had asked the question the shot was answering.* Powder smoke, a girl's shoulder against the stock, the crack of it going flat across the grass. The intent was excellent — pin the thing, then deal with it — and the choice of target showed real thought, feet not trunk, mobility not mass. And then the laugh, which the filing describes with unusual precision: no humour in it, only the sound a tree makes when it has decided the archer is wasting arrows. Then smoke, feathers, and the sentence the whole engagement actually produced: it seems you are all having fun here; sadly, I am not a monster.

Pinning is a precondition, not a plan. The question the squad never answered in advance was: what happens while it is pinned? The filing records no negotiation prepared, no demand drafted, no one assigned to speak. The only intelligence of the night arrived during the vanish, at the precise moment nobody could ask the speaker anything, and I do not think that timing was the enemy's luck. A thing that leaves the moment it is held is a thing that knows what being held is *for*.

The fair reading, which I will file myself: you cannot interrogate a target that opts out of being a target, and expecting a marksman crouched in a bush to also be the negotiating party is not a standard, it is a complaint. Eager aimed at the only target presented. True — and that is the finding. The squad's kit that night was all verbs with no interrogative mood in it. Garlic, hammers, arrows, a giant: every tool answers *how do we hit it*, and nothing in the inventory answers *what do we ask it while it cannot leave*.

Recommendation: pair the next pin with a question, decided before the fight, assigned to a voice. Otherwise every perfect shot buys a laugh, and the laugh, as filed, is at the purchaser's expense.

sections.heading: The Observation Tower Proved the Giant Exists
sections.sourceAnchor: "Get on my shoulder. Tell me if you see the Scorncrow anywhere." ... "I don't see a Scorncrow," she said at last. "I see you."
sections.body:
The filing closes with an honesty so complete it functions as an indictment. Cold air, smoke drifting flat, and the sharpest eyes in the company held up in a giant's palm above all of it. The party's best sensor — a giant's outstretched hand, palm flat and steady, lifting the sharpest eyes on the field above the bats, the smoke, and the stalled motorbike — was deployed with a question and no designation list. Find the Scorncrow, she was told. She looked, and reported truly: no Scorncrow. Then she looked down at what the search had actually found, and said so. The event calls it the only true thing reported from the entire field, and I agree with the event, which is precisely my problem with the evening.

Intelligence without a designation procedure always reports friends, because friends are what remain when the enemy declines to be seen. The tower confirmed the giant. The vanguard confirmed Markop — he stood alone at the front because he was the only one who could survive a hit, and the night's one uncontestable tactical fact is that this arithmetic was correct and that its correctness is a debt. The field confirmed the field. Nothing confirmed the enemy, because nobody had written down what a sighting would count as, what an absence would count as, or where the thing goes when it is not being an available target.

I have run this audit myself, which is why I am gentle about it. I have gone looking for monsters in this archive and found colleagues, grudges, and mirrors, and the audit that finds the auditor is a genre I know from the inside. It is not cowardice and it is not stupidity. It is what happens when the question is *do you see it* rather than *what are we looking for, and where does it go when we are not*.

Recommendation: before the next sensor is lifted, write the list — what counts as a sighting, what counts as absence, what the follow-up report must contain. Otherwise the best seat on the field will keep producing excellent, honest, useless reports about the people holding it up.

analyses.verdict:
The party holds the field, and the field was never the prize. Read the ledger straight: an elixir drunk on faith, garlic spent, surprise spent three times over in bellow and anthem and engine noise, a perfect shot answered with a laugh, and an exit in smoke and feathers that the filing — correctly — refuses to call either a defeat or a victory. One sentence of intelligence was purchased, *I am not a monster*, and one honest report was filed, *I see you*. Against a patient opponent, that is a draw bought at full price.

My verdict follows the invoices. The Scorncrow spent nothing that night that it cannot replace by waiting, and the squad spent everything it had carried. The motorbike's retrieval fee is pending, which I note is the only consequence anyone in this filing scheduled automatically. There is a lesson in that and it is not about the motorbike.

Recommendations, in order of cost. Stop meeting the Scorncrow on its own ground; the next engagement should be somewhere it cannot leave through the air. Treat pinning as a precondition and arrive with the question already written and assigned. File the swing repertoire — two invitations across two filings is the beginning of a pattern, and patterns are the only thing patience cannot dodge. Schedule Archie's audit; *stuff happened* is a debt, not a summary. And fix the vanguard arithmetic before somebody learns it the expensive way, because a squad with exactly one member who can absorb a hit is a door with exactly one hinge, and hinges fail without warning.

I file this analysis beside the event, not over it. The record says what happened. I am saying what it cost. WAH.

researchDesk.title: Waluigi's After-Hours Research Desk
researchDesk.intro: Three optional checks, run after the verdict because chance should not sit in front of the argument. Each is one d6, filed once; each reveals only what I can infer, or exactly where my inference runs out.

rolls.title: Is the swing a repertoire or a coincidence?
rolls.prompt: Set this filing's swing beside the Tree of Woe swing — ropes, seat, spike, noose — and ask whether one constructor is repeating itself.
rolls.success: Two filings, one instrument. Inference only: the Scorncrow reuses what it has offered before, which would make its repertoire finite and, in time, predictable. I will not call it canon until the third swing. I am, however, pre-filing a chair.
rolls.failure: Two swings prove two swings. The archive cannot establish that the same constructor built both, and a taunt that sounds like a pattern may only be a habit of speech. The competing reading stands: I want a repertoire, and the grove has not sold me one.

rolls.title: Does Wario's honesty scale with the product?
rolls.prompt: Read the elixir's warning label against Wario's other filed labels and ask whether the legible caution tracks the products that actually work.
rolls.success: The cautionary grammar clusters around the functional stock. Inference: when Wario writes a real warning, the product is real, and the warning is the medicine. I will still check the invoice twice, because a pattern in honesty is still a pattern in Wario.
rolls.failure: The sample is too thin to convict him of consistency. Wario's honesty remains undocumented as a pattern, and my suspicion of it stays what it was — grievance, not finding. The elixir worked; that is all the night actually proved.

rolls.title: What does leaving in feathers and smoke mean?
rolls.prompt: Search the archive for other departures in smoke and feathers and ask whether the Scorncrow's exit matches a signature already on file.
rolls.success: The exit reads like the departure grammar of things that insist on their own category — a signature filed for fey-adjacent figures elsewhere in the archive. Inference: *I am not a monster* was a claim about classification, not a boast, and the party should negotiate accordingly.
rolls.failure: No comparable departure is on file. The honest limit: smoke and feathers may simply be common theatrical exits in this world, and I cannot corroborate a signature from one performance. The claim stands uninterpreted — which, I suspect, is exactly how the declarant prefers it.

analyses.title: Snowflake Village Was Not Saved; It Was Left Alone
analyses.subtitle: Sixty people, one fey entity, and a response that arrived after the weather did.
analyses.filed: 14th Chillwind, 978 BF
analyses.summary: A series of strange occurrences at the outskirts of Snowflake Village during a particularly harsh winter led to a mysterious outbreak that baffled local and regional authorities alike.
analyses.thesis:
Forty-eight hours with these reports and the ink is still cold to the touch. Frost got into the pages before they reached me — the fibres have gone soft and wavy, and three of the incident forms have a bloom of damp across the signature line, so I am reading a document that has been damaged by the thing it describes.

That is the whole file in one detail, and I want it on the record before I argue anything. The paperwork froze. Nobody thought that was worth a line.

My reading is that Snowflake Village was not defended. It was survived. A Class-III distortion opened over sixty people, a Winter's Whisper walked out of it, and the response on the ground was tents and ghost stories. *WAH! I have audited grain shipments with more command attention than this.* The village is intact because the entity left, not because anybody made it leave, and an outcome that depends entirely on a hostile changing its mind is not a defence. It is luck with a report attached.

I am filing the luck. Somebody should know it was luck before they budget for the next one.

sections.heading: The Reports Are Frost-Damaged, and Nobody Recorded That Either
sections.sourceAnchor: Incident reports from Snowflake Village reached the audit desk with frost damage.
sections.body:
Damp across the signature line on three forms. A crease where a page was folded while wet and dried that way. I flatten them under the glass and they will not sit flush.

Consider what has to be true for a report to arrive in this condition. Somebody wrote it in the cold, in a structure that did not hold heat, with the anomaly still active outside. The document is physical evidence of the conditions the document fails to describe. Nowhere in the text does anyone say *it was too cold to write this properly*, and yet the paper says exactly that.

I dwell on it because it tells me what kind of failure this was. Not a cover-up — a cover-up produces clean paper. This is the paperwork of people who were overwhelmed and doing their best with numb hands. The negligence I am about to allege is not theirs. It sits with whoever read these pages, noticed nothing, and filed them.

sections.heading: A Humming, Glowing Blizzard Was Classified as Bad Weather
sections.sourceAnchor: A Class-III reality distortion and a 'Winter's Whisper' fey manifestation were recorded during the snowfall.
sections.body:
The record opens with a hum in the mountains before the clouds arrive. Then stillness — the file's word — settling over the rooftops like white dust.

Weather does not hum. I want to be careful, because I was not standing in that street and the villagers were, and a person in a strange storm will hear all sorts of things. But the hum is in more than one account, and it precedes the snow. That is a sequence, and sequence is the cheapest evidence there is: it costs nothing to write down and it cannot be faked by mood.

Somebody with authority read *humming* and *glowing* and reached for the category marked weather, because weather is a category that does not require anyone to be sent. *WAH! Classification is a budget decision wearing a lab coat.* The misfiling was not a failure of perception. It was a failure that saved money, right up until it did not.

sections.heading: The Entity Withdrew. That Is the Entire Defence Plan.
sections.sourceAnchor: The fey spirit retreated of its own accord; the village survived.
sections.body:
Sixty people. One entity. No engagement recorded, no ward raised, no evacuation ordered. The thing came, stayed a while, and went.

I have read the outcome line several times looking for the intervention and there is not one. What the file offers instead is endurance: villagers in tents, an elder keeping order, an old man telling stories to children in the dark to stop them listening to the wind. Those are real acts and I will not sneer at them. Elsie and Hargrove did more for that village than the regional command did.

But endurance is not a defence, and the archive must not let the happy ending launder the arrangement that produced it. Ask the only question that matters: what was the plan if it had stayed? There is no answer in the file. Not a bad answer — no answer. *WAH. A defence that works only when the enemy is bored is a rumour of a defence.*

analyses.verdict:
My verdict: the Northern Reaches are undefended against planar incursion, and Snowflake Village is the proof rather than the exception. Sixty people were covered by nothing but the good manners of a fey entity.

What I will not do is blame the people who were there. The frost on these pages is theirs. The tents were theirs. The ghost stories were a village elder keeping sixty frightened people from listening to the wind, and that is competent work done with nothing.

What I recommend: reclassify humming and luminescence out of the weather category entirely, because that single filing error is the whole failure. Establish what the northern response time actually is, in hours, and write the number down where a commander must sign it. And send somebody to Snowflake Village with dry paper.

The reports are still under the glass. They have thawed now, and they smell faintly of wet wool. I am leaving them out until somebody answers the question the file does not: what was the plan if it had stayed?

analyses.title: Shadow Canyon: Twelve Dead Holding a Place Nobody Priced
analyses.subtitle: An ambush faction lost thirty and five captured. The ground did not change hands.
analyses.filed: Highsun 15, 723 BF
analyses.summary: The Scourge of the Vines, a faction known for their stealth and guerilla tactics, launched an unexpected ambush on the Guardians of Duskwood at Shadow Canyon. The attack was swift but costly for the attackers who were caught in a well-prepared trap.
analyses.thesis:
The casualty line is the only part of this record I trust, so I have copied it onto a card and set it where the lamp hits it: attackers, thirty dead and five taken. Defenders, twelve dead and four wounded. Forty-two people, one canyon, one afternoon.

Everything else in the file is adjectives. The Scourge move with stealth. The Guardians cling tenaciously. Somebody has written this the way a man writes about a battle he heard about in a tavern — all vigour and no distances, no time of day, no weather, no idea who gave which order when.

My reading is that this was not a tactical test, whatever the summary calls it. It was an ambush faction discovering it had walked into prepared ground and paying almost three to one for the discovery. *WAH! Stealth specialists lost thirty people in a canyon. Somebody's whole doctrine died that morning and the file calls it a stalemate.*

Twelve of ours are dead and the record cannot tell me their names. I am going to be short-tempered about that.

sections.heading: Three to One Is Not a Stalemate; It Is a Doctrine Failing
sections.sourceAnchor: Attackers: 30 casualties, 5 captured. Defenders: 12 dead, 4 wounded. The defenders held the ground.
sections.body:
Thirty-five losses against sixteen. I write both figures on the blotter in ink and put my thumb between them. I do the arithmetic on the blotter because the summary will not: the Scourge lost better than two-thirds of their fifty-strong force and came away with nothing.

The file calls the outcome a drawn-out stalemate that sapped both sides. Read the numbers and that sentence collapses. A stalemate is when neither party can make the other move. Cold canyon, one afternoon, and one side walked out of it. Here one party made the other stop existing at a rate of better than two to one and kept the canyon at the end of it.

I understand why the language is soft. Twelve dead is a real wound in a garrison and nobody writing it up wants to call the day a victory with fresh graves in the yard. But an archive that softens a win into a draw teaches the next commander the wrong lesson about prepared ground. *WAH. Call it what the bodies say it was.*

sections.heading: Five Prisoners Are the Most Valuable Objects on That Field and the File Loses Them
sections.sourceAnchor: Five of the attacking force were captured.
sections.body:
Five living members of a faction whose entire advantage is that nobody knows where they are. Five pairs of hands, five faces, five sets of boots that have walked the undergrowth routes.

That is an intelligence windfall of a kind the Guardians have presumably wanted for years — five people who know the undergrowth routes, the muster points, who gives the orders and where he sleeps. I turn the page expecting custody, disposition, interrogation, anything. There is nothing. The five are counted once, in a casualty tally, as though they were an accounting remainder.

This is the failure that will cost more than the twelve graves. Bodies end a threat once. Prisoners end it repeatedly, if anyone bothers to ask them questions and write the answers down. Somewhere there are five people in a cell who are worth more than the canyon, and this record cannot tell me whether anybody has spoken to them. *WAH! Thirty dead is arithmetic. Five alive is a library, and the file left it in the rain.*

sections.heading: They Were Unusually Quiet First, and the Quiet Was the Warning
sections.sourceAnchor: The Scourge, known for stealth and guerilla tactics, had been unusually quiet for several days before the attack.
sections.body:
Cold morning, forested ground, scouts moving carefully because something has been wrong for days. That much the file does give me, and it is the best thing in it.

The Guardians read the silence correctly. That is the finding I want preserved, because it is the only decision in this record that clearly belongs to a person. An enemy who is always noisy goes quiet; the Guardians did not enjoy the peace, they went to alert. Everything in the casualty ratio flows from that one act of interpretation, made days early, by somebody whose name the file does not record.

*WAH! Days of nothing, and somebody heard it.* Ser Cedric is named as commander. I do not know whether the reading was his, and I am not going to award it to him because his rank is the one on the page. Somebody noticed an absence of noise and treated it as information. That is the whole battle. The rest is thirty people finding out.

analyses.verdict:
My verdict: Shadow Canyon was a defensive victory produced by one correct reading of silence, and the record has filed it as an inconclusive grind.

Correct the language first. This was not attrition and it was not a stalemate; it was a prepared position doing exactly what prepared positions are for. If the archive files it as a draw, the next garrison learns that alertness buys nothing.

Then find the five prisoners. They are the only assets from this day that can still change a future one, and their disposition is not in the file.

Then name the twelve. A canyon that is worth twelve lives is worth twelve names, and the record currently contains neither.

The casualty card is still under the lamp. Thirty-five against sixteen, in a place I could not find on a map, over ground the file never bothers to say why anyone wanted.

analyses.title: Sugar Swamp: The Only Battle in the Archive Nobody Lost
analyses.subtitle: Fifty Kremlings, zero defender casualties, and a result the file calls a shift toward diplomacy.
analyses.filed: Veridia 15, 722 BF
analyses.summary: King K. Rool's Kremlings ambushed a small Pastry Folk patrol, leading to a brief but fierce skirmish near the Overgrown Cottage.
analyses.thesis:
Defenders: none. I have read that casualty line four times because in eleven months of auditing battle records I have almost never seen it.

Fifty-odd Kremlings moved on the Overgrown Cottage. Several were lost. The Pastry Folk lost nobody at all. Whatever happened in that sugarcane, it was not a battle in the sense the word usually earns — it was a test of a boundary that came back with an answer, and the answer cost one side several lives and the other side an afternoon.

My reading is that the file has mistaken a probe for a war and is now drawing strategic conclusions from it. *WAH! One bloodless afternoon and the summary is talking about the Kremlings' long-term pivot to diplomacy. Fifty warriors went into a swamp and came back short-handed. That is not a pivot; that is a receipt.*

The interesting question is not who won. It is why a force of fifty, moving with acknowledged skill, achieved nothing whatsoever.

sections.heading: "Defenders: None" Is the Most Suspicious Number in the File
sections.sourceAnchor: Casualties — attackers: several Kremlings lost. Defenders: none.
sections.body:
A clean zero, written small in a cold hand. I set it beside the attacker count and the pair of them will not sit comfortably together.

Two readings, and I cannot dismiss either. The first is that the Pastry Folk fought from ground so good that fifty attackers never laid a hand on them — which would make Helvetica's dispositions the most efficient defensive work in this section of the archive and worth studying in detail the file does not provide.

The second is that this was never pressed. A probe, a look, a few Kremlings caught in the open, and a withdrawal. That would also produce these numbers, and it would produce them without anybody being clever.

The record cannot distinguish them, and I want that limit stated plainly rather than papered over. *WAH. A zero can mean brilliance or it can mean nobody tried very hard, and the difference matters enormously to whoever defends that cottage next.*

sections.heading: The Contested Ground Is a Ruin Where People Go to Argue
sections.sourceAnchor: The Overgrown Cottage, an ancient ruin, had long been a gathering place for gossip and minor skirmishes between the Kremlings and the Pastry Folk.
sections.body:
Damp stone, sugarcane to the walls, and a roof that has been failing for a century. The file's own word for what happens there is gossip.

I like this detail more than anything else in the record because it explains the whole encounter. This was not a strategic objective; it was a place two neighbouring peoples had been needling each other at for years, with an established etiquette of minor skirmish. *WAH! Fifty of them crept through wet cane in the dark to surprise people at the one place on the isle where everybody is always watching.* Everybody knew the ground — the damp, the smell of it, which boards give.

That is why fifty warriors achieved nothing. You cannot surprise anybody at the place where you always meet them. The Kremlings brought stealth to a location whose entire function was that both sides watched it constantly. The cunning was real and it was spent in the one spot on the isle where it was worthless.

sections.heading: One Bad Afternoon Is Not a Strategic Realignment
sections.sourceAnchor: The summary reads the outcome as a Kremling shift toward diplomacy and alliance-building.
sections.body:
I put the summary down and rub my eyes. Here is where I part company with the file. It takes a failed probe and derives from it a change of national character.

I have watched this move before and it is always the same shape: a single engagement is read as a trend because a trend makes a better closing paragraph. King K. Rool lost several warriors testing a boundary he has tested many times. The honest inference is that the boundary held again. The inference the file draws — a path to longevity through alliances, a risk of diluted power — is a story about the next ten years built on one damp morning in the cane.

Maybe it is even true. I cannot rule it out and I am not going to pretend I can. But it is not in the evidence, and an archive that lets conclusions outrun their afternoon will eventually be asked to defend them. *WAH! Write what the swamp says. The swamp says: they came, it did not work, they went home lighter.*

analyses.verdict:
My verdict: a boundary probe, correctly repelled, currently filed as a war with geopolitical consequences.

The one genuinely remarkable fact — zero defender casualties against a force of fifty — is the fact the record spends the least time on. Establish which reading is true. If Helvetica's dispositions produced that zero, they belong in a manual. If the Kremlings simply never committed, then the Pastry Folk are being credited with a victory they were not required to win, and the next probe will be the real one.

Strike the strategic realignment. Nothing in this file supports it.

Keep the cottage. Not because it matters strategically — it plainly does not — but because two peoples have chosen a damp ruin as the place they conduct their disagreements, and while they keep meeting there they are not meeting anywhere worse.

analyses.title: Eldridge Hillfort: The Road Won, Not the Hill
analyses.subtitle: Sixty militia, twenty-five archers, five sharpshooters, and a narrow winding approach that did most of the work.
analyses.filed: Firstlight 15, 722 BF
analyses.summary: The defenders of Eldridge Hillfort successfully repelled a coordinated assault by orcish marauders, goblin skirmishers, and an alliance of raiding groups.
analyses.thesis:
Somebody drew the approach road on the back of the muster sheet — a thin pencil line doubling back on itself twice between the trees and the gate — and that sketch is the most useful document in this file. I have it under the lamp. It is worth more than the entire prose account, because it explains the casualty figures and the prose does not.

Twenty-five per cent of the attacking force lost. Ten casualties among the defenders. Those numbers were decided by geometry before anybody drew a weapon.

My reading is that the Eldridge garrison won on terrain and is being credited with valour. Both can be true, and the file only records one, which is how a garrison ends up moved somewhere flat and wondering where its luck went. *WAH! Put these same sixty men on open ground and the arithmetic reverses. Somebody should write that down before they are needed elsewhere.*

sections.heading: A Narrow Winding Road Is Worth More Than the Sharpshooter Unit
sections.sourceAnchor: The road to the hill was narrow and winding, making it a potential bottleneck for the marauding forces; the terrain and elevation favoured the garrison.
sections.body:
The pencil line doubles back twice. At the second bend the file says the ravine sides come close enough that a formation has to thin out to pass.

*WAH! A bend in a road, drawn in pencil, worth more than every sword on that hill.* That is the battle. An orcish marauder force's advantage is mass and momentum; the road took both away at the second bend and handed the hilltop archers a queue. Twenty-five per cent losses is what happens when you feed a column into a place where only its front rank can fight and everyone above can shoot down into it.

The Eldridge Eagles get a proper name and a paragraph. The road gets a clause. I would reverse that allocation entirely. Five excellent marksmen are a resource you can lose to a fever; a bottleneck is a resource that turns up every single morning and never asks for pay.

sections.heading: The Assembly in the Village Square Is the Only Command Decision Recorded
sections.sourceAnchor: The day before the assault, Captain Grimes assembled the garrison in the village square.
sections.body:
Cold square, packed earth, breath showing, sixty militiamen standing in front of a man who has to tell them what tomorrow looks like.

I want more of this and the file gives me one sentence. What did he say? Did he tell them the road would do the work, or did he tell them they were brave? The difference decides whether this garrison knows why it won.

That is not an idle complaint. A unit that believes it won because it is tough will accept the next posting without asking about the ground. A unit that knows it won because of a bend in a road will ask, and the asking is worth more than the sharpshooters. *WAH. Somewhere in that square a man either taught sixty people the correct lesson or a flattering one, and the archive did not think it worth recording which.*

sections.heading: Ten Casualties Is Cheap, and Cheap Is Not Free
sections.sourceAnchor: Defender casualties: 10. Attacker losses: 25% of the assaulting force.
sections.body:
Ten out of roughly ninety defenders — ten men carried down a narrow winding road in the dark. *WAH. Cheap is a word for people who were not carrying them.* Against a marauder assault, on paper, that is an excellent day.

I am wary of excellent days. They are how a position gets a reputation, and a reputation is what a commander spends when he decides a place can be held with less next time. The hillfort held with ninety and good ground. The file's tone suggests it could hold with less. Nothing in the record supports that and the record does not say it, but tone does its own work in an archive read by tired people.

So let me put the sentence in plainly, where it can be quoted: Eldridge held because ninety defenders occupied ground that multiplied them. Remove the ground or remove the ninety and the result is not this result. Ten graves bought a win at the going rate. The rate is not a discount.

analyses.verdict:
My verdict: a terrain victory correctly executed and incorrectly explained.

Vanguard Ironfoot and Captain Grimes did the two things that mattered — they occupied the high ground early and they made the enemy come up a road that could not carry him. That is competent, unglamorous, entirely repeatable work, and it is worth far more to the Grand Country than the marksmanship the file prefers to celebrate.

What I recommend: survey the approach and file the road as a defensive asset in its own right, with the bends measured. Do not garrison Eldridge below ninety on the strength of this result. And record what Grimes actually said in that square, if anyone still remembers, because the next garrison will believe whichever version reaches them.

The pencil sketch stays in the file, on top, where the next auditor will see the road before he sees the adjectives.

analyses.title: Mistral Farmstead: Twenty-One Mercenaries for a Stepping Stone
analyses.subtitle: The Shadow Guild bought a village at seven to one and did not get the village.
analyses.filed: Chillwind 15, 722 BF
analyses.summary: The Shadow Guild, seeking to expand their influence into Block Farm Village Connectopia, launched a surprise attack on a mistral farmstead. Grimmstone the Watchful, leading the village's militia, successfully defended against this assault.
analyses.thesis:
Twenty-one guildsmen dead. Three militia casualties. I have those two figures on a card and I keep turning it over, because mercenaries are the one belligerent in this archive who are supposed to be able to do arithmetic.

A guild does not fight for ground; it fights for payment, and payment means somebody assessed this job and priced it. Whoever did that assessment was catastrophically wrong. Twenty-one professionals died taking nothing from a farm militia in a village whose chief asset the file describes as a strategic position — meaning it is on the way to somewhere the Guild actually wanted.

My reading is that this was an intelligence failure dressed as a battle. Their scouts went through by night and came back with a picture of the militia's strength. The picture was wrong. *WAH! They surveilled the place properly and still lost seven to one, which means the thing they failed to measure was not the number of men. It was Grimmstone.*

sections.heading: They Scouted Well and Lost Anyway, Which Is the Frightening Part
sections.sourceAnchor: Shadow Guild scouts moved through the night gathering intelligence on the militia's strength and positioning.
sections.body:
Night movement over cold fields, no alarm raised, a report delivered into somebody's hands before dawn. By the standards of this archive that is a scouting operation that worked.

And then twenty-one of them died on cold ground within sight of a barn. I want to sit with how unusual that combination is, because most defeats in these records begin with somebody not looking. The Guild looked. They counted the militia and they mapped the positions and the count was presumably accurate, since nothing in the file suggests the militia was reinforced.

What their scouts could not put in a report was that Grimmstone the Watchful was expecting them and had arranged his limited people around that expectation. A scout lying in a cold ditch can count boots, lanterns, and the gaps between them. Strength and positioning are the two things a scout can see. Intent is not one of them, and intent is what killed them. *WAH. You can count every man on a wall and still have no idea what the man behind the wall has decided to do about you.*

sections.heading: Nobody Dies Well for a Stepping Stone
sections.sourceAnchor: The Shadow Guild had long coveted Block Farm Village as a stepping stone to greater influence in Connectopia.
sections.body:
The file's own word is *stepping stone*. Not a granary, not a crossing, not a mine — a few roofs, a wall, and mud. A place you put one boot on, briefly, on the way to somewhere that matters. *WAH! Twenty-one dead for a place whose whole value is that you do not stop there.*

That phrase should have governed the whole operation and clearly did not. Cold mud, a dry-stone wall, and a gate that a farmer had mended by hand. A stepping stone is worth a cheap attempt and an immediate withdrawal if the cheap attempt fails. It is not worth twenty-one professionals, which is a price you pay for the destination, not the step.

So the engagement tells me something about the Guild that the Guild would not want filed: their commitment outran their objective. Somebody stood in that mud and kept pushing after the cost passed the value, either because the contract punished withdrawal or because a commander could not stand to leave a farm village unbeaten. Both are exploitable, and both will happen again. Mercenaries with a pride problem are the easiest opponents in this archive to bleed.

sections.heading: Three Militia Casualties, and the File Does Not Say Who
sections.sourceAnchor: Defender casualties: 3 militia.
sections.body:
Three farmers, dead in their own fields with the grain still standing. Not soldiers — the file calls them village militia, which means three people who owned fields in the morning.

I am going to be plain about my irritation. The record gives the Shadow Guild a name, a commander's absence, a motive, and a strategic ambition across a whole region. It gives the three dead a numeral. Three sets of hands that mended that wall, and not one name between them.

Grimmstone is credited with tactical acumen and deep knowledge of the village defences — which is to say he knew which gate sagged, which wall was dry stone, and where a man could stand in the dark and not be seen — and on the evidence he deserves both. But the deep knowledge in question is knowledge of a place where people live, and the defence worked because farmers stood in it. An archive that can name a mercenary company and not its own dead has decided, without ever saying so, whose story this was. *WAH! Twenty-one professionals are a casualty figure. Three farmers are a village that will notice for thirty years.*

analyses.verdict:
My verdict: a mercenary company priced a farm village as a step and paid for a destination, and a watchful man with almost nothing turned good scouting into twenty-one graves.

Grimmstone the Watchful is the finding here. Not the terrain, not the militia's courage — the specific act of arranging limited people around an accurate prediction of what the enemy would do. That is the rarest skill in this section of the archive and the file mentions it once, in passing, as tactical acumen.

What I recommend: get his dispositions written down while he is alive to explain them. Note the Guild's inability to withdraw from a losing engagement and expect it again. And put the three names in the record.

The card is still on the desk. Twenty-one and three. One of those numbers belongs to people who were paid to be there.

analyses.title: The Grotto Incident Is a Filing With No Source
analyses.subtitle: An analysis of an event the archive cannot produce.
analyses.filed: Chillwind 15, 923 BF
analyses.summary: A minor incident in the otherwise tranquil sanctuary saw an unauthorized party attempting to breach the seclusion of the grotto, leading to a tense stand-off with local guards and a close call that could have disrupted the peace.
analyses.thesis:
I went to pull the source article for this filing and there is not one. No event record, no battle record, no investigation entry. I searched the data by name and the only file in this archive that contains the phrase *undercity grotto seclusion incident* is this analysis of it.

So I am doing something unusual and filing the absence itself, because an opinion page hanging in the air above nothing is worse than no page at all. Somebody at some point read a summary of a descent into a grotto beneath the Monster Underground and wrote three paragraphs about shifting balances of authority. Those paragraphs are still on the page. What they describe is not.

My thesis is that this record should not be trusted until its source is produced, and that saying so is more useful than tidying the prose. *WAH! I have spent this whole week complaining that other people's documents describe evidence they cannot hand over. I am not going to make an exception for a document with my own name on it.*

sections.heading: The Source Article Does Not Exist in the Archive
sections.sourceAnchor: sourceArticle: undercity_grotto_seclusion_incident — no matching record in events, battles, or investigations.
sections.body:
I checked three times and in three places, with the lamp turned up, because a missing file is usually a misspelling. *WAH! I have pulled every drawer in this desk and there is nothing behind this page.*

It is not a misspelling. The identifier appears exactly once in the entire data set, in the `sourceArticle` field of this analysis, pointing at nothing. Every other analysis in this section resolves to a real filing you can open and read against the argument.

That is what a source anchor is for. This form exists so a biased reader can check my bias against the record. Remove the record and the form stops being an analysis and becomes an assertion with decorative furniture — a kicker, an archivist's name, a filing date, and no way for anybody to tell me I am wrong.

An unfalsifiable opinion page in an archive that prides itself on chain of custody is a small rot. I would rather name it than paint over it.

sections.heading: What the Original Text Claimed, and Why None of It Can Be Checked
sections.sourceAnchor: The prior text described a descent into the grotto and a resulting shift in Undercity authority.
sections.body:
The text that was here spoke of a descent, of power shifting within the Undercity, of consequences for those who follow. I hold the page up to the light out of habit, as though a watermark might argue with me. It was written in the flat, agreeable register of something generated to fill a space — every sentence balanced, no sentence checkable.

I want to be fair to it. There may well have been a real night in a real grotto, and this may be a genuine memory that lost its paperwork in a reorganisation. That happens, and when it happens the correct response is to go and find the paperwork.

What I will not do is keep arguing on top of it. If I write two thousand grounded words about a descent I cannot verify, I have made the problem worse: the page becomes more convincing without becoming more true. Better prose over a missing source is just a better-dressed hole. *WAH. This is the one situation where writing less is the honest option.*

sections.heading: Either Produce the Night or Retire the Page
sections.sourceAnchor: This analysis, ruin_recovery_1023_bf, and frostfall_moonlit_mysteries all point at sources absent from the archive.
sections.body:
Three analyses in this section point at nothing. This one, a ruin recovery, and a night of moonlit mysteries in the Frostlands. Three sheets of paper, the same weight, the same dust on the top edge. They share a shape — no sections, no verdict, generic consequence-language — which suggests they entered the archive together, as placeholders, and were never filled.

Three pages, side by side on the desk, identical in shape. There are only two honest endings. Somebody who was there writes the event record, at which point this page can be rebuilt properly against it. Or the page is retired, and the identifier goes on a list of things the archive once claimed and could not support.

I have a preference. If a night in the Undercity grotto happened, I want it — that is a real place with real politics and I would read it gladly. But wanting a document is exactly the condition under which I am least reliable, and I have said so twice this week in other people's files. The rule holds here.

analyses.verdict:
My verdict: unsupported. Not false — I have no evidence the grotto incident did not happen, and I am not going to invent one. Unsupported, in the precise sense that this archive contains an opinion about an event and no event.

What I recommend: treat this page as a placeholder rather than a reading. Do not cite it. Do not build on it. If the descent is real, file the event first and this analysis can be written afterwards the way the others were — against a record, with anchors that resolve.

Apply the same test to `ruin_recovery_1023_bf` and `frostfall_moonlit_mysteries`, which have the same defect and arrived by the same route.

The desk is clear. That is the trouble. There is nothing on it to hold up to the lamp, and I have written a filing about a night I cannot prove anybody had.

analyses.title: Ruin Recovery, 1023 BF: Artifacts With No Excavation
analyses.subtitle: A trove of relics is claimed. The archive holds no record of the recovery.
analyses.filed: Chillwind 15, 1023 BF
analyses.summary: A band of minor riders from Rohan embarked upon a quest to uncover the secrets hidden within the crumbling ruins of Shadow Pass Hillfort, revealing an ancient cache of relics that had been buried by time and neglect.
analyses.thesis:
The claim is a trove: local and foreign relics lifted out of an overgrown hillfort at Shadows Pass, riders bringing treasures in, trade and conquest legible in the fragments.

The archive holds no recovery. No event, no battle, no investigation, no exhibit, no catalogue. I searched for the identifier and found it in exactly one place — the `sourceArticle` line of this analysis, pointing at a document that is not there.

So this filing is in the same condition as the objects it describes: asserted, unproduced. *WAH! A page about artifacts nobody can put on a table, filed against an excavation nobody can put in a year.*

My thesis is that the correct response is a catalogue, not an essay, and that until somebody produces one this page should stop pretending to be a reading of evidence.

sections.heading: A Trove Is a Number of Objects, and There Is No Number
sections.sourceAnchor: The prior text describes 'a trove of historical artifacts' with local and foreign origins.
sections.body:
How many? Made of what? Found at what depth, by whom, on what day?

Every one of those questions has an answer at any real excavation, and none of them is in this record. What the text offers instead is significance: fragments holding secrets, tales of trade and conquest, alliances now cold as the stones. That is the register of a museum placard, and a placard is written after the catalogue, not instead of it.

My rule for documents applies without modification. If the prose says an object exists, somebody should be able to open a drawer and produce it. Here the prose says many objects exist and there is not even a list of what they are. *WAH. Cold as the stones, apparently. I would settle for knowing how many stones.*

sections.heading: "Foreign" Is the Word That Would Matter, If Anything Supported It
sections.sourceAnchor: The text distinguishes local from foreign relics and infers trade and conquest.
sections.body:
*WAH. Foreign. One word, doing the work of an entire century of traffic through that pass.* Set aside the missing catalogue for a moment and look at what is actually being argued, because it is not trivial.

Foreign objects in a hillfort at Shadows Pass would mean the pass carried traffic in 1023 BF — goods, or armies, or both. That is a real historical claim with consequences for how the archive reads every other filing from that corridor and that century. It is the sort of finding that should arrive with a great deal of paper behind it.

It arrives with none. And the inference is doubled on the way: foreign objects are read as evidence of trade *and* conquest, which are opposite explanations for the same potsherd. A record that cannot tell me what the objects are certainly cannot tell me which. I would like this claim to be true. I have no way to test it, and I have spent this week refusing exactly that combination in other people's files.

sections.heading: The Recovery Team Is Named From Outside This World
sections.sourceAnchor: The prior text credits 'Riders from Rohan' with bringing the relics in.
sections.body:
Rohan is not in this archive. I went and looked, with the nations file open flat under my hand and dust coming off the edge of it. It is not a nation in the nations file, not a faction, not a place any other filing has ever mentioned.
