researchDesk.intro: The verdict is filed. These three checks pull at the parts of the tape I cannot close from the chair. A breakthrough sharpens the reading; a dead end gets filed as an honest limit, because a limit written down is worth more than a guess dressed up.

rolls.title: Find the hand that cut the tape
rolls.prompt: The silhouette passage is an editorial choice and so is the ending. Work the physical tape - splice marks, generation loss, duplication artefacts - and ask who had it before I did.
rolls.success: Breakthrough: the silhouette passage sits a generation cleaner than the footage on either side of it, which means it was not filmed that way - it was composited in later from a second source. Somebody had two recordings of this argument and built one tape out of them.
rolls.failure: Dead end, filed honestly: the tape is a copy of a copy and the wear is even enough that I cannot separate an edit from a dropout. I cannot prove the cut. I can only prove that I cannot prove it.

rolls.title: Place the shadow at the window
rolls.prompt: A figure watched the softest thirty seconds of this argument from outside and was gone before the shouting resumed. Establish the hallway's geography and work out what could physically be standing there.
rolls.success: Breakthrough: the window in frame is above ground level on that elevation. Whoever was in it was not walking past. They were positioned, and they left when the tone changed rather than when the argument ended.
rolls.failure: Dead end: the silhouette carries no detail I can scale against the architecture, and I will not build a witness out of a smudge. Logged as present, unidentified, uninterviewed.

rolls.title: Audit the Cape Feather against the greed reading
rolls.prompt: Set the feather beside Wario's reframing. A mobility item drawn at the lethal beat, and then a month of absence. Test whether flight and keeping are the same story.
rolls.success: Breakthrough: the feather is not a defensive draw. Cross-referenced against the fountain timeline it puts Mario airborne and eastbound inside the window the courier's note describes - which makes the note a forwarding address rather than a distress call.
rolls.failure: Dead end: a man reaching for an escape item while his brother promises to kill him is not evidence of anything except fear. The greed reading survives the night but it does not gain a witness.

analyses.title: The Roll Call at Trinity: A New Advisor, Eleven Names, and the Word Nobody Was Supposed to Explain
analyses.subtitle: The archivist argues the disclosure was an accident, the accident was the best thing that happened all morning, and the bill for it fell on a girl who never asked to be mentioned
analyses.filed: 5 Aethel, 1040 BF — evening, from the desk, with the classroom record and a cold cup of tea
analyses.summary: My reading is that nothing in that classroom was planned, including the only useful thing in it. A confused newcomer asked what a word meant, an advisor who could have let it die answered instead, and eleven children learned what they belong to. I credit him for that and I bill him for what it cost.
analyses.thesis:
The classroom record is on my desk, eleven pages of it, and I have been through it three times because the first two passes gave me the wrong answer. The first pass says: introductions session, low stakes, nothing happens. The second says: institution briefs students, standard. Neither survives the third.

Here is my argument. **Every consequential thing in that room happened by accident, and the institution was not steering any of it.** The class learned it was attached to SCHALE because somebody who did not know better asked. The Equestrian programme entered the record because somebody looked up in a corridor. A student's weapons clearance became public because a man wanted emphasis in an argument he had already won. Not one of those three disclosures was a decision. They were all leaks, and two of them cost somebody something.

I was not there. I have never been to Kivotos. What I have is a transcript of a morning, and transcripts are where institutions confess by accident, which makes this exactly my kind of document.

sections.heading: The First Confession Was In The First Minute, And It Was A Joke
sections.sourceAnchor: "Because if you're comparing me to your last advisor who 'mysteriously disappeared,' I assure you — I'm much harder to get rid of."
sections.body:
I have the line in front of me, and I have put my thumb on it, because it is the sentence I keep coming back to at this hour.

A man walks into a classroom he has never taught, on his first morning, and within sixty seconds makes a joke about his predecessor having *mysteriously disappeared* — in air quotes, which the record specifies. He does this to eleven children he has not yet named.

And nobody laughs. Nobody gasps. **Nobody asks.**

That is the part that keeps me at the desk. A joke only works if the room already has the information, and this room had it. Every child in 2-B knew that the last adult in that job went missing, knew it well enough that it needed no setup, and had evidently reached a settlement with the fact long before this man arrived. An institution had absorbed a disappearance so completely that it had become a punchline available to a stranger on day one.

I want to be careful here, because I am aware of what I want this to mean. I would *like* it to mean something sinister, and I have been wrong in that direction before — I spent three filings reading a scarecrow's confession as villain theatre. So let me hold to what the document supports: an adult attached to a SCHALE operational classroom is unaccounted for, the students treat this as old news, and the replacement was comfortable enough to joke about it.

One of those three facts is strange. All three together are a file, and I have opened one.

sections.heading: The Most Important Thing In The Session Was Asked By Somebody Who Did Not Know Better
sections.sourceAnchor: A voice from the floor: "SCHALE operations?"
sections.body:
Two words. That is the entire mechanism.

The advisor had said *SCHALE operations, academy life, the whole package* as throat-clearing, the way an administrator says a thing he assumes is furniture. And a newcomer — somebody with no social investment in appearing to already know — said **SCHALE operations?** back at him.

I have spent a long time around institutions and I can tell you precisely what should have happened next. That question should have died. The room was noisy. The man had a clipboard and a rotation to get through. A deflection here costs nothing: *we'll get to that*. I have watched a hundred officials execute that move and I have never once seen one penalised for it.

He put the clipboard down instead. Deliberate click — the record notes the click, and I note that the record notes it. He turned to face the room fully. He held up a hand to stop an interruption. And he answered.

I am not in the habit of crediting men with clipboards, so let me get it over with: **that was better than the average and I am saying so in writing.** The whole of this archive's first view inside Kivotos exists because one man declined an easy dodge in front of witnesses who could not have called him on it.

Now. Everything that is wrong with this filing is also downstream of that decision, and I will spend the rest of the page on it, because credit given is not credit owed forever.

sections.heading: He Told Children Who The Enemy Is And Gave Them No Way To Check
sections.sourceAnchor: "They're criminals who want to tear down everything Kivotos stands for — the academies, the peace agreements, all of it."
sections.body:
He wrote THE RESISTANCE on the board in block capitals. He underlined it twice. Then he said that sentence.

I have read it eleven times tonight and my objection is not the one you expect. **I am not saying it is false.** I want that in bold because the cheap move here is for the archivist to side with the insurgency on principle, and I have covered enough insurgencies to know how many of them are precisely what the state says they are. It may be exactly true.

My objection is procedural, and it is worse than a disagreement. *Not one person in that room had the means to test it.* Eleven students, one of whom had just admitted nobody had ever explained the basic architecture of his own school to him, received the moral status of an armed political faction as a single declarative sentence from the only adult present. They could not have pushed back. They had nothing to push with.

That is not a briefing. A briefing gives you enough to assess a claim. This gave them a conclusion and the authority of a man at a whiteboard, and then moved on to logistics.

So the archive files it as **his characterisation** — attributed, dated, in his words — and not as a finding about the Resistance. I have written *ask again in twenty sessions* into the event record and I meant it as an instruction to myself.

And note the grammar he closed on: *You — all of you — are part of that.* Not *will be asked*. Not *may volunteer*. **Are.** Past tense of a decision no child in that room remembers making.

sections.heading: He Broke Need-To-Know Ninety Seconds Before He Explained It
sections.sourceAnchor: "—except Tsurugi. You already have clearance." A beat. "Everyone else: no."
sections.body:
This is the passage that made me put the transcript down and walk around the room, and I am going to be plain about why.

Somebody asked whether the class could have guns. Two seconds of silence, and the person who filled them was the girl in the back with her boots on the desk — the one who had contributed a *keheh* and two complaints all morning. She uncrossed her arms, pointed at the adult like a blade, and said that if the answer was yes then this class is an excuse for a shooting range and she would be **filing paperwork**.

Read that again. The most responsible position taken by anybody in that room, adult included, was taken by the delinquent, and she took it *against her own interest*. She is the one person present with weapons experience. A yes makes her the most important student in 2-B. She argued no anyway, and her threat was not violence. It was a form.

The advisor got it right — *nobody is handing out guns* — flat, final, correct.

Then he held up a finger to preempt an objection she had not made and was not making, and added that she already has clearance.

She did not volunteer that. It is nowhere in the record that she offered it, hinted at it, or invited him to confirm it. He took a fact that belonged to her, about the one capability that will define how ten classmates see her, and spent it as rhetorical punctuation in an argument he had already won by a mile.

**And then he turned to the whiteboard and wrote NEED-TO-KNOW and underlined it twice.**

Ninety seconds. I could not have built a cleaner demonstration with a year and a budget. The record shows no reaction from her at all — no *keheh*, no *what a pain*, nothing — and after three passes I think that silence is the most informative thing in the document.

sections.heading: The Liaison Programme Did Not Fail By Being Secret. It Failed By Being Seen
sections.sourceAnchor: "So the fact that you saw them walking around openly tells me someone dropped the ball on security protocols somewhere along the line."
sections.body:
A student mentioned seeing pony liaisons in the school. The record catches the advisor's face doing something — jaw tightening a fraction — and then the clipboard going down with that same deliberate click he uses before saying something he will have to defend.

He confirmed it. Cultural exchange with Canterlot, small groups, goodwill in advance of anything needing formal coordination. *Supposed to be handled quietly.* He could have denied it and did not, and by the standards I applied above he deserves partial credit again.

But hold the sentence he actually produced up to the lamp. The failure he identifies is **that the students saw**. Not that a school full of minors was hosting foreign diplomatic personnel without being told. Not that the escort schedule slipped. The incident is the observation.

And the remedy he issued follows exactly from that framing: report further sightings *to me — not to social media, not to your friends, to me. Directly.* In one move he converted eleven children into an informal observation network aimed at their own school's guests, roughly ninety seconds after informing them they were part of SCHALE.

I am not even angry about it. I am impressed by the speed. But I know what I am looking at, and so does the girl in the corner, who stopped writing, put something in the margin that was not part of the lecture, said *…Understood* to nobody, and went back to work. I would give a great deal to read that margin. I suspect this archive eventually will.

sections.heading: The Only Structure Anybody Chose That Morning Was A Committee About Clothes
sections.sourceAnchor: "An alliance. They're forming an *alliance* over a cape."
sections.body:
Every serious thing in this session was imposed. The attachment, the rotation, the enemy, the clearance disclosure. The children were told.

So watch what they built when left alone for four minutes: an outfit-design committee with no remit, no authority and no institutional existence whatsoever. Asa Hanko proposing. Airi escalating to balloons on tactical gear. Hanae supplying logistics nobody requested. Lord Verity blessing it in the third person. Yoshimi refusing to join it and then, in the *very next breath*, producing a crumpled pamphlet and announcing she had finished page six.

I want to defend this properly, because the easy read is that the class is unserious and the easy read is wrong.

Hanae had gone home after a single briefing, cross-referenced the SCHALE material against the school's emergency protocols, colour-coded it, and **found gaps in the documentation**. Nobody asked her to. Yoshimi had read the only copy of the terms anybody in the room possessed and spent the entire session waiting for a reason to say so. Airi crossed the floor twice to reach the two students nobody was talking to. Tsurugi, offered balloons, produced the only warm sound she made all morning.

An institution told these children they were part of an operation and declined to say what it was for. They responded by constructing the only thing in that room that belonged to them. I have seen adults do considerably worse with considerably more.

sections.heading: Two Questions Were Asked Out Loud And The Record Shows No Answer To Either
sections.sourceAnchor: "…Doesn't matter though. I'm not on any list. Supplementary students don't count for much either way."
sections.body:
I am going to stop performing for a moment. The voice is a tool and this is not the place for it.

Shirasu Azusa — corner desk, angled away from the room, pen parallel to the notebook edge — asked whether SCHALE actually works, or whether it is another thing that sounds important and does nothing for people already at the bottom of every list. Then she said she is not on any list at all, and that supplementary students do not count for much either way.

I have checked the record four times for a reply. There is none. The lecture continued.

Iochi Mari — who had earlier stopped a riot with one polite sentence and no authority whatsoever — raised a hand she did not need to raise and asked whether any of this means the class will get to *do something meaningful*, because people do not care about gadgets or uniforms, they care about purpose.

The record does not show him answering that either. It shows him dropping into his chair and setting the order of business: deployment rotation first, then fashion.

Eleven people and one adult heard both questions. Both were audible. One received silence and the other received a rotation.

An institution that will not answer *does this do anything for me* has answered. I have filed that sentence in two separate places in the event record specifically so it cannot be lost underneath the balloons, and I will be asking both questions again, in writing, every session, until somebody in that building says something.

analyses.verdict:
**This is a good room, and it is a room where a fourteen-year-old said she does not count and eleven people let it pass.** Both halves are my finding and I will not trade either for the other.

The advisor is better than the average of his profession. He answered a question he could have killed, he conceded his employer's name is nonsense, he refused to arm children, and he admitted a diplomatic failure rather than denying one. I have audited a great many institutional men and most of them would have done none of those four things.

He also handed minors a verdict on an armed faction with no evidence attached, framed a secrecy breach as a visibility problem, recruited his students as informal observers, and broadcast a girl's weapons clearance to win an argument he had already won — then wrote NEED-TO-KNOW on the board and underlined it twice.

My recommendation is that the archive stops treating candour as the whole of honesty. This man told the truth about nearly everything, which is exactly why the children will believe the one sentence he had no business saying.

**Three things are owed and I have opened leads against all three:** account for the previous advisor of Classroom 2-B; obtain the terms of the Canterlot agreement and the outcome of the visibility query; and establish what the supplementary classification actually does to a student, because one of them already believes she knows and nobody in authority contradicted her. WAH.

researchDesk.title: Waluigi's After-Hours Research Desk
researchDesk.intro: Three optional checks, filed after the verdict because dice have no business in front of an argument. Each is one d6, once. Each returns either a sharper inference of mine or the exact place my inference stops.

rolls.title: Was the advisor post filled in a hurry?
rolls.prompt: Set the joke about the disappeared predecessor beside the roll sheet — a bare list of names with no faces, read badly enough that one entry was ticked against the wrong student.
rolls.success: Inference only, and it is mine rather than the record's: a man given names without faces and no briefing on a class that had just lost an advisor was posted in a hurry, which means the vacancy was urgent and the school had no better candidate to hand.
rolls.failure: It stops here. First-day registers are routinely bare, and a hurried posting and a merely disorganised one produce identical paperwork. I cannot separate them from this document.

rolls.title: Did the two programmes meet at Trinity by accident?
rolls.prompt: Put the quiet Canterlot exchange beside the SCHALE operational attachment of Classroom 2-B and ask whether one building is carrying an improbable amount of significance.
rolls.success: Supplemental inference: a school hosting both an unannounced diplomatic programme and a newly operational SCHALE classroom is either the most important building in its district or the most convenient one, and both readings make Trinity a target rather than a campus.
rolls.failure: An honest limit. Trinity is large and prominent, and the dull explanation — that everything in Kivotos meets there because everything in Kivotos meets there — fits the evidence exactly as well as mine does.

rolls.title: Does somebody already hold a file on Tsurugi?
rolls.prompt: Read clause 6.3 of the pamphlet — restricted equipment only under certified instruction by certified personnel — against a student who arrived at this classroom already cleared.
rolls.success: Inference: her clearance predates this advisor and was issued by a body with a certification record, which means an institution somewhere holds a file on a Trinity student that Trinity did not open and this advisor had plainly not read before he announced its contents to her classmates.
rolls.failure: The limit is real. Clearance may sit with an authority that has no obligation to a school, and its existence tells me nothing about who holds the paperwork or whether anyone at Trinity may ever see it.

analyses.title: Judgement in the Grove: A Musket in the Smoke, the Warhammer That Would Not Hear an Appeal, and the Man Remi Found Asleep
analyses.subtitle: The archivist argues the party did not win an argument in that grove — it ended one, and the archive is poorer by exactly one witness
analyses.filed: After 1 Aethel, 1040 BF — filed late, rewritten twice, because the first version was angrier than it was useful
analyses.summary: My reading is that the killing was lawful, defensible, and the single most expensive act of the arc. A disarmed prisoner mid-sentence is the most informative object this party has ever held, and it was converted into a corpse and a secondhand scythe. I am not moralising. I am invoicing.
analyses.thesis:
It is late and I have the grove filing open beside the two Scorncrow files that precede it, which is the only way to read it honestly.

For three filings I wrote that *I am not a monster* was taunt. Mine is the name on those pages. Then Remi put a musket against its face at point-blank range, the face came away, and the blood underneath was human — and I had to correct myself in public, which is the only way an auditor is permitted to do it.

So understand that when I come to the grove I am not arriving neutral. I arrive as the man who got it wrong in the direction of *it is only a monster*, watching a party arrive at the same conclusion with a warhammer.

**My argument is narrow and I will hold it all the way through: the kill was defensible and the timing was catastrophic.** Those are separate findings. Almost everybody who discusses this filing collapses them, and the collapse is how the actual loss goes unrecorded.

sections.heading: Count What The Party Was Holding At The Moment Of The Swing
sections.sourceAnchor: Disarmed, unmasked and on its knees, it identified itself as human and formally asked a paladin for mercy.
sections.body:
I have the sequence written out on a card on my desk, because the sequence is the whole argument and it is very easy to lose inside the noise of a battle filing.

At the moment the warhammer came down, the party held: a combatant **disarmed** — scythe out of reach, not in hand. **Unmasked** — the hood off, the human face plainly visible, twice-confirmed by a musket eleven days earlier. **Kneeling.** **Speaking.** And speaking not threats but a request, addressed by name to the one member of the party whose entire vocation is the adjudication of mercy.

That is not a monster at the end of a fight. That is a **witness**, in custody, voluntarily talking.

I have spent my career trying to get objects into that condition. Do you know how rare it is? Everything else in this arc dissolves, burns off, reverts, or laughs and flies away — this one stayed, on its knees, mid-sentence, in a posture no one had to maintain by force.

Whatever else is true about that morning, the party was holding the most valuable object of the entire Shadeward arc, and it held it for the duration of one swing.

sections.heading: I Will Defend The Kill Before I Bill It
sections.sourceAnchor: The Scorncrow had been in the record for three engagements and never once stayed for the end of a fight.
sections.body:
Let me argue the other side properly, because an auditor who only prosecutes is a fan with a grievance.

This thing had been in the record for three prior engagements and had **never once stayed for the end of a fight.** It vanished at the Tree of Woe. It was carried off by crows over ground Archie had made unsafe. It laughed at a critical hit into its own roots and left. Its entire established method was to disengage the instant an encounter turned against it.

So a paladin looking at a kneeling Scorncrow is not looking at a settled prisoner. He is looking at the one thing in the arc that has always, always escaped — currently motionless, in a grove that is itself hostile terrain, with the party's own casualties on the ground behind him. Salam went down in that fight and did not get up.

And the appeal itself is not neutral evidence. A creature that has spent three engagements performing — the laugh, the swing, the playground invitation — asking for mercy in the precise words it has been shouting as a taunt is, at minimum, an ambiguous document.

**I do not think Markop murdered anyone.** I think he made a fast decision about a proven escape artist with his own wounded behind him. Put me in that grove and I do not trust the kneeling either.

Now the bill.

sections.heading: The Cost Is Three Readings The Archive Can No Longer Choose Between
sections.sourceAnchor: Two separate tests, eleven days apart, both returned human.
sections.body:
Here is what that swing bought, itemised.

Before the grove, the archive had three live readings of *I am not a monster*: something human is **inside** the scarecrow, wearing it, willing or otherwise. Something human **was made into** it, and the sentence is a complaint. Or the blood is a costume too, and I am being played by a thing that learned what this party finds persuasive.

After the grove, the archive has **exactly the same three readings**, and no remaining means of separating them.

That is the entry. Not a moral one — an evidentiary one. The kill cost nothing in the field; the party held the ground and the grove is open. It cost everything in the file, because the one instrument capable of distinguishing those three readings was a human being with a mouth, and he was using it at the time.

I want to be exact about my own position, because I can hear how this sounds. **I am not saying they should have let it live.** I am saying that somewhere between *disarmed* and *dead* there was a window in which one person could have asked one question — *what are you* — and that the window closed without anybody reaching for it.

The archive does not get to reopen it. That is the loss, and it is mine to record because I am the one who spent three filings making the same mistake more slowly.

sections.heading: It Picked The Paladin, And That Is Either Instinct Or Research
sections.sourceAnchor: It went down on its knees and asked Markop — a paladin, chosen deliberately — for mercy.
sections.body:
This is the detail I keep returning to at this hour, and I have not settled it.

There was a whole party in that grove. It addressed the paladin.

Two readings, and I can argue both. The first is instinct: a frightened human in a field of armed strangers picks the one in holy armour because that is what holy armour is *for*, and the choice means nothing except that he was afraid and could still see.

The second is worse and I cannot dismiss it. This creature had fought these specific people three times. It had watched Dan turn spiders with a mushroom-studded holy symbol. It knew the composition of this party. A thing that studies its opponents and picks, from among them, the single individual whose oaths make refusal costly — that is not a dying reflex. **That is a last, well-aimed move by something that had been paying attention the entire arc.**

And note which reading is more frightening, because it is not the one people expect. If it was calculating, it lost — Markop refused and it died anyway. If it was *sincere*, then a human being correctly identified the one person in the clearing whose job was mercy, asked him for it in plain words, and was killed mid-sentence by exactly the man he had chosen.

I cannot tell you which. Neither can anybody else now.

sections.heading: The Only Paperwork The Execution Generated Was An Inventory Line
sections.sourceAnchor: Markop took the scythe off the body.
sections.body:
I have the field ledger in front of me and it is a perfectly competent document, which is the problem.

Item: one scythe, stolen origin. Taken from: the Scorncrow, deceased. Taken by: Markop. Condition of prior holder: **kneeling**.

That is the archive's entire formal record of a killing. A form designed to track equipment, carrying a word about a man's posture at the moment of his death, because there was no other field to put it in.

I am not being sentimental. I am making a records point that this archive keeps having to relearn: **the shape of the document decides what survives.** An inventory line has a slot for the object and no slot for the appeal. So in a hundred years, when somebody pulls the Shadeward file, the scythe will be exhaustively documented — origin, custody, current holder — and the question of what was under the hood will be three competing paragraphs written by an interested party at midnight. Me.

That is why I opened an exhibit against it and why I wrote the observation note on the human face as a separate document. Not because either tells us anything the party does not know. Because in fifty years the ledger will still be legible and the memory will not, and I refuse to let the only durable record of that morning be a line about a farm tool.

analyses.verdict:
**Defensible act, catastrophic timing, and the bill lands on the archive rather than on the paladin.** That is my finding and I have rewritten this page twice to make sure it is not merely my temper.

Markop killed a proven escape artist that had never once stayed to the end of a fight, with his own wounded on the ground behind him, in hostile terrain, using a judgement call he had perhaps two seconds to make. I decline to convict him of anything, and I note he is the second person in this arc to be judged harshly for acting fast — I was the first, and I was wrong then too.

What I will not do is pretend the ledger balances. The party was holding a disarmed, unmasked, kneeling, *talking* witness — the rarest object this arc has produced — and the encounter ended with three unresolved readings, one corpse and one secondhand scythe. The thing that died was human. It said so four times. Twice we tested the claim with weapons and twice the claim held.

My recommendation is concrete and I have filed it as a critical lead: **identify the body.** There is a human face in the Skittering Grove that nobody has matched against a missing-persons record. If he was taken and made into that, somebody is still waiting for him. If he wore it willingly, the grove recruits locally. Both answers change what we think the grove is, and the corpse is now the only place either answer lives.

Stop calling it the monster. It told us four times that this was the wrong word, and the one time anybody tested the claim with a firearm, the claim held up. WAH.

researchDesk.title: Waluigi's After-Hours Research Desk
researchDesk.intro: Two optional checks, filed behind the verdict where chance belongs. One d6 each, once, and each returns either a sharper inference of mine or the honest edge of it.

rolls.title: Was the appeal a tactic it had used before?
rolls.prompt: Set the grove appeal beside the three prior engagements — the playground swing offered to a child, the laugh at a critical hit, the exits in smoke and feathers — and ask whether this creature had an established habit of offering things to people.
rolls.success: Inference only: the swing at the Tree of Woe was also an offer made to someone it had no obligation to address, which would make the appeal to Markop the same instrument pointed the other way — and the last item in a finite repertoire.
rolls.failure: My limit, and it is a real one. An offer under no threat and a plea under a warhammer are not the same act, and reading one as evidence of the other is pattern-matching by an archivist who wants a pattern.

rolls.title: Would a missing man of that description be on any list?
rolls.prompt: Take the two physical findings — human blood, human face, remains that stayed remains — and ask what jurisdiction would hold a missing-persons record for the area around the Skittering Grove.
rolls.success: Supplemental inference: the grove sits in territory where the Iron Legion has been operating and filing, which means somebody near that ground keeps lists, and a lawful request for them is a thing this party could actually make.
rolls.failure: An honest stop. Rural disappearances in contested ground are frequently never reported at all, and an absence from any list would prove nothing except that nobody was in a position to miss him.

analyses.title: The Tape and the Wario Files
analyses.subtitle: The archivist has already read what the tape says; this is the reading of where it came from, which nobody has asked about and which he now cannot stop asking about
analyses.filed: Filed after the line-by-line reading, late, once the obvious question had finished not going away
analyses.summary: I have written at length about what is on this tape and I stand behind all of it. This page is about the part I skipped: a private argument between two brothers was recorded by somebody, reached the archive through a man who sells things, and has no origin at all. Nobody has asked. I am asking.
analyses.thesis:
The cassette is on the desk in front of me, squared to the blotter, spine label blank. I have played it more times than is good for me and I have already filed the line-by-line reading — the one where I argue the fight is not about betrayal but about being seen. I do not withdraw a word of that.

But here is what has kept me at this desk since: **I built that entire argument on an object with no beginning.**

The tape enters the archive already in Wario's possession. Before Wario there is nothing. No recordist, no room, no instruction, no chain. And then — after I had published my reading of the poor copy — a materially cleaner dub surfaced, source unstated, and I amended my filing like a good auditor and did not once ask who had been sitting on the better one.

That omission is mine. This page is the correction.

sections.heading: A Two-Voice Argument Does Not Record Itself
sections.sourceAnchor: A primary source at last — the brothers' argument, in their own voices.
sections.body:
Put your hand on the physical object for a moment, the way I have mine now. It is a tape. Tapes require a machine. Machines require a person to start them, and — this is the part that should have bothered me a year ago — a person to **place** them.

The recording is clean enough that I built a line-by-line reading on it. I distinguished tone. I heard where Mario answers the wrong question. That is not what a device forgotten in a drawer across a room produces; that is a capture from somewhere near the conversation.

So: somebody chose a room, chose a moment, and chose a placement, for a private argument between two brothers.

I can think of three people it might have been and I am going to name none of them, because naming suspects in an archive is how an archive becomes a rumour. What I will commit to is the structural claim: **the most important document in the Mario file was created by a deliberate act, and the actor is not in the file.**

Every conclusion I have drawn about that argument sits on top of that absence. Including the conclusions I like.

sections.heading: The Better Copy Arrived After I Published, And That Is Information
sections.sourceAnchor: Revised same week, once a cleaner dub of the tape surfaced and I heard how much I had missed the first time.
sections.body:
I wrote, in my own filing, that an auditor who does not correct his own work is not an auditor but a fan. I meant it and I acted on it.

What I did not do — and it is the kind of omission I would prosecute in anybody else — is note what the arrival of a second, better copy *implies*.

It implies **copies exist**. It implies somebody made them. And it implies somebody decided when this archive would receive the good one, which was: after reading what I concluded from the bad one.

Now, I can hear the reasonable objection, and it is mine as much as anyone's: dubs surface for extremely dull reasons all the time. Somebody finds a box. A better machine turns up. An archive that reads intent into every delivery will eventually read intent into a postal delay, and I have mocked people for less.

But the dull explanation requires a coincidence — that the improved copy happened to appear in the same week that a widely-read reading of the inferior copy was published. I am not able to make that coincidence feel small.

So I record it as a live possibility rather than a finding: the disclosure may have been **responsive rather than cooperative.** Somebody may be reading what I file and adjusting what I get.

sections.heading: The Custodian Is A Man Whose Entire Method Is Transaction
sections.sourceAnchor: Held by Wario, prior to disclosure.
sections.body:
I am about to be accused of family bias, so let me get in front of it: Wario is not a liar. He is something much more useful to an investigator and much worse for a chain of custody — he is a **dealer**. Things come into his possession and things leave it, and the governing question is always price rather than truth.

That matters here in a specific way. A dealer does not need to forge anything to distort a record. He simply needs to decide *when* to produce a genuine object, and to whom, and in what condition. Every one of those decisions is a thumb on the archive's scale, and none of them is a lie.

He produced a real tape. The tape is authentic — I have staked my reading on it and I stake it again here. But an authentic object released at a chosen moment by a man who trades in leverage is not the same thing as evidence freely given, and the archive has been treating it as though it were.

I notice, too, that nobody asked him. Not in the filing, not in the sessions around it, not by me. A man handed us the single most consequential document in the Mario disappearance and the entire company's follow-up question was *play it again*.

I have played it again. Six times, by the curtains-drawn count in the filing. It is time somebody asked him where he got it.

sections.heading: I Have Played It Six Times And The Sixth Taught Me Nothing New
sections.sourceAnchor: Midnight, second day, sixth rewind. The curtains have not been opened since the clinic.
sections.body:
The filing's own image is a man in a chair at midnight on the second day, sixth rewind, curtains still shut since the clinic. I recognise the posture because I am currently in it.

And I want to put something uncomfortable in writing, because this page is supposed to be where I am honest rather than merely correct.

**The sixth rewind taught me nothing the third had not already.** By then I was not listening for information. I was listening because the voices were there and the room was quiet and stopping the tape meant going back to a file where Mario is still missing. That is not research. That is company.

I raise it because it bears directly on the provenance question. A document you have played six times stops being a document. It becomes furniture — a thing so familiar that asking where it came from feels like an insult to an old friend. That is precisely how an archive ends up building two filings on an unexamined gift: not through carelessness, but through **intimacy**. You do not interrogate the chain of custody of something you can recite.

So take this section as a methodological confession attached to a case note. The reason nobody asked Wario where he got the tape is that by the time anybody thought to, the tape no longer felt like evidence. It felt like ours.

It is not ours. Somebody made it, somebody kept it, and somebody chose the hour we heard it clearly.

sections.heading: None Of This Weakens The Reading, And I Will Not Let It Be Used That Way
sections.sourceAnchor: Read line by line, the fight is not about Mario at all.
sections.body:
I want a firewall here, because I know how provenance arguments get misused and I have no intention of handing anybody that tool.

Questioning where a document came from is **not** the same as questioning whether it is true. The tape's content is corroborated by its own internal texture — two voices that know each other's history, a fight with the specific ugly shape that only real fights have, and a line of Luigi's that no forger inventing a corruption story would have thought to include because it does not serve one.

My line-by-line reading stands. Luigi is not asking to be forgiven; he is asking to be **acknowledged**, and Mario keeps answering a question nobody asked. I believed that when I had the poor dub and I believe it more with the clean one.

So let the record be exact about what this page claims and what it does not. It does not claim the tape is doctored. It does not claim the argument went differently. It claims one narrow thing: **we do not know who wanted us to hear this, and that is a fact about the case which is currently recorded nowhere.**

An unknown benefactor is still an unknown. Two filings of conclusions rest on a gift, and nobody has looked the gift in the mouth.

analyses.verdict:
**The tape is true and its provenance is a hole, and the archive has been treating the first fact as though it settles the second.** It does not.

I stand fully behind my line-by-line reading. The argument is about being seen, Mario loses it by answering the wrong question, and the impostor-derived versions the archive carried for two filings were wrong. None of that is in question here, and I will not have this page cited by anyone trying to reopen it.

What I am filing is a gap. Somebody deliberately recorded a private argument between two brothers. Somebody made copies. Somebody handed one to a dealer, or the dealer was there himself, and somebody chose to release a cleaner version only after reading what I had concluded from the worse one. Not a single link in that chain is documented, and I built two filings on top of it without once writing the words *where did this come from*.

My recommendation is the plainest in this archive: **ask Wario.** He is available, he is not hostile, and nobody has put the question to him. Then establish who produced the second dub and when it was made, because a copy has a date and a date has a person attached to it.

Until then I am attaching a standing caution to my own best work: every conclusion in the Mario file currently rests on a gift from an unidentified giver. WAH.

researchDesk.title: Waluigi's After-Hours Research Desk
researchDesk.intro: Two optional checks, run after the verdict as the form requires. One d6 each, filed once. Each returns a supplemental inference of mine or the precise point at which I stop being able to argue.

rolls.title: What does the audio quality say about where the machine sat?
rolls.prompt: Consider that the capture is clean enough to support tone analysis of two distinct speakers throughout a moving argument, and ask what that requires of the recorder's position.
rolls.success: Inference only: a capture that holds both voices intelligibly through a mobile argument implies a machine placed centrally and deliberately rather than one running by chance in a corner, which narrows the recordist to someone with prior access to that room.
rolls.failure: Honest limit. I am an auditor, not an engineer, and the surviving copy has been dubbed at least once — which means the qualities I would reason from may belong to the copying rather than the original.

rolls.title: Was the cleaner dub released in response to my filing?
rolls.prompt: Place the publication date of my first line-by-line reading against the week the improved copy surfaced, and ask whether the sequence supports a responsive disclosure.
rolls.success: Supplemental inference: the improved copy appearing only after a widely-read reading of the inferior one is consistent with somebody monitoring this archive's output and metering what it receives — which would make the holder an active party rather than a source.
rolls.failure: This is where I stop. Two events in one week is a sequence, not a mechanism, and I have publicly mocked people for building conspiracies out of exactly this much.

analyses.title: The Snowdin Bone-Line Registry
analyses.subtitle: The filing asks whether the interview was real. This asks a narrower and worse question: who is the author of a family, and what happens to an archivist who notices he has been doing the same job
analyses.filed: Filed after the registry event, once the comparison had become impossible to avoid
analyses.summary: The event file ranks three readings of what happened in Sans's room and declines to choose. This page does not revisit that. It takes the third reading seriously for one page and asks what it would mean — because if a document can constitute a family rather than record one, then the difference between Times New Roman and me is a difference of effect, not of method.
analyses.thesis:
I have read this interview eleven times and the thing that keeps me at the desk is not the fire, the wing, or the vanishing. It is **entry #472.**

[Times New Roman](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/times_new_roman) logs Sans's puns. He has them numbered. Asked who authorised it, he said no permission was required, because it is *an archival initiative.*

I have said that sentence. Not a similar sentence — that one, in that register, to people who asked why they were in this encyclopedia. I keep a file on a man who has never spoken to me. I have filed children, corpses, and a rock.

So the question this page asks is not *was the registry real.* The question is: **what is the operational difference between documenting a family and constituting one, and am I on the safe side of it?**

I do not reach a comfortable answer.

sections.heading: Twenty-Eight Records Cited A Document That Did Not Exist
sections.sourceAnchor: Twenty-eight filed dossiers cite the Snowdin household registry as their authority.
sections.body:
Start with the administrative fact, because it is stranger than anything that happened in the room.

Twenty-eight dossiers — [Papyrus](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/papyrus), [Grandpa Semi](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/grandpa_semi), [Pet Rock](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/pet_rock), all of them — carry the line *recorded in the Snowdin household registry.* Each cites the registry as the thing that establishes it.

**The registry did not exist when those lines were written.** Not sealed, not lost. Unwritten.

In any ordinary archive that is a sourcing failure and I would spend a page being rude about it. But look at the order of operations here. The citations came first. The document came second, and it came into existence during an interview conducted *because* of the citations.

A record that is summoned into being by the volume of references to it is not behaving like evidence. It is behaving like demand.

sections.heading: Two Relatives Are Made Out Of Things Sans Said About His Brother
sections.sourceAnchor: 'If you cheat, you'll end up a dirty brother.' 'My brother has a very special attack.'
sections.body:
Both quotations are confirmed. Sans said them, about [Papyrus](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/papyrus), years apart, in ordinary circumstances. One was a warning against taking a shortcut. One was a compliment.

The archive holds a dossier for [Dirty Brother](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/dirty_brother) and a dossier for [Has A Very Special Attack](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/has_a_very_special_attack).

Sans's reading is that somebody built relatives out of his sentences. It is a good reading and I want to be clear that he arrived at it unprompted, in real time, while being shown edited footage — he identified the hard cut at *'my brother will—'* before I could.

But hold the two dossiers side by side and something uncomfortable emerges. Dirty Brother is **soot-covered because he repairs boiler shafts, chimneys and old puzzle mechanisms.** That is not a slander built out of an insult. That is a working life, with a trade in it.

A fabricator working from the phrase *dirty brother* invents somebody disgusting. Whoever filed this one invented somebody **employed**. That is either unusually careful forgery, or it is not forgery.

sections.heading: Kinship Asserted By Reference Number, With No Parent Anywhere
sections.sourceAnchor: 'Designation: brother. Confirmed by archival lineage code #TNR-01.'
sections.body:
Consider what is *missing* from the sibling-designation instrument. No mother. No father. No shared childhood, no location, no date of a birth or an adoption. A document that establishes brotherhood and declines to mention a parent.

What it has instead is **#TNR-01**, footnotes, and an appendix reference for skeletal alignment.

A lineage code implies two things the archive cannot produce: an **issuing authority**, and a **register older than the code**. Neither has been identified. Sans, asked directly who his mother is, says [Toriel](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/toriel) — a goat, who baked pies, and is not on the instrument at all.

So the instrument does not descend from a family. It descends from a **filing system**. And the man holding the pen is the filing system's clerk.

sections.heading: A Document That Consumes Itself Is Doing Something, Not Recording Something
sections.sourceAnchor: The contract ignites. Silent blue flame. Names curling to ash shaped like small bones.
sections.body:
This is the hinge and I want to go slowly.

Sans signs. The instrument burns. **Then every name on it walks into the room**, [Gee Lady](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/gee_lady) opening the light that admits the rest, and [Wing Gaster](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/wing_gaster) resolving at the back of it.

Records do not do that. A record is inert; that is the entire virtue of a record. You may consult it, dispute it, or lose it, and it does not answer.

This one required **consent** — a signature, in a blank box, from the one member who had spent the whole interview refusing the document. Then it destroyed itself in the act of being completed. Then its contents arrived.

[Times New Roman](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/times_new_roman) watched it burn **without reacting**. Not shock, not grief at losing a document he had just produced. The composure of a man watching an expected step complete.

I file the plain reading: the burn is not destruction. It is **execution**, in the sense a contract is executed.

sections.heading: Entry #472, And The Question I Would Rather Not Have Asked
sections.sourceAnchor: 'No permission required. This is an archival initiative.'
sections.body:
Here is the comparison, stated plainly, once.

Times New Roman keeps an indexed chronicle of a household. He numbers his entries. He distrusts any account that begins *you had to be there.* He documents people who have not consented and considers the question of consent irrelevant to the work. When challenged he invokes the initiative rather than a right.

Every clause of that paragraph is also true of me.

The distinction I would like to claim is that **my records do not summon anybody.** I file a dossier and the subject does not thereby exist; they existed first and the dossier is late. That is the whole difference, and it is a difference of *effect*, not of method or of ethics.

Which leaves an unpleasant residue. If the third reading is correct — if this registry constitutes — then Times New Roman is not a worse archivist than me. He is a **more effective one**, doing the identical job with a better instrument.

I have elected not to find out whether the difference is one of kind or merely of degree. I note that electing not to find out is itself a choice, and that I have made it about the one experiment that would settle the question.

analyses.verdict:
**The registry is not a genealogy and should stop being read as one.** It is an instrument, and the filing should treat it the way it treats every other instrument: by asking who issued it, who benefits, and what it does when executed.

On the evidence: it asserts kinship by a code with no issuing authority; it names no parent while its subject names a mother who is not on it; it required consent from the one participant who had spent an hour refusing it; it destroyed itself on receiving that consent; and it was immediately followed by its own contents arriving. Every one of those properties belongs to instruments, not to records.

**What I will not claim** is that this makes the Bone-Line false. Two of the entries are built from Sans's own sentences, and one of those two came out with a trade attached that no insult would have supplied. A family that is constituted is still a family. Pet Rock is on that tree and Sans carries Pet Rock in his pocket.

**What I withdraw** is the comfortable position. I opened this page intending to argue that Times New Roman is doing something I am not. I cannot locate the clause where that becomes true. The honest finding is that the difference between his archive and mine is that his works, and I have chosen not to test mine.

WAH.

rolls.title: What body issues an archival lineage code?
rolls.prompt: #TNR-01 implies a register older than itself. Cross the numbering against the Snowdin Chronicle Office's other output.
rolls.success: The numbering is sequential from 01 and Times New Roman holds it. A register whose first entry is its own archivist is not inherited — it was **opened**, by him, and everything filed since descends from that act.
rolls.failure: The Chronicle Office produces no other numbered series I can obtain from outside the Underground. The code may be authentic, self-issued, or decorative, and I cannot separate the three.

rolls.prompt: Audit the twenty-eight dossiers for any evidence of the subject having been consulted.
rolls.success: Not one of the twenty-eight records a consultation. Twenty-seven were written without asking Sans, who appears on every version of the tree. The single member who has consistently refused the paperwork is the member every piece of paperwork depends on.
rolls.failure: Consent is not a field the archive keeps, on any record, including mine. I cannot audit for the absence of a thing I never thought to record.

analyses.title: The Shepherd's Garden and the Three-Week Clock
analyses.subtitle: One question only: the Oracle chose the moment to describe Peach's death, and the moment he chose was the one at which his listener had just been proven unable to check
analyses.filed: Filed after the commentary, once the sequencing had stopped looking accidental
analyses.summary: The event files the disclosure and the commentary rules the Oracle a source rather than a witness. Neither asks the narrower question: why that hour. This page argues the timing was the deliverable — that an hour of engineered provocation was not a character test but a **fitness check on an audience**, and that the assassination account was released the instant it passed.
analyses.thesis:
Everybody has been reading the order of events as: provocation, then confession.

Read it the other way. **The provocation was qualification.** The [Oracle](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/the_oracle) insulted Bowser's importance, barred his path, offered a poisoned shortcut, and finally named Peach — and then told him, afterwards, that it had been a test and that half of it he had not meant.

A man who wanted to unburden himself does not run a four-stage diagnostic first.

What the diagnostic established is precise and it is not *is Bowser trustworthy.* It is: **will this man swing, will he walk out, and can he verify anything I say.** The answers were no, no, and no. The account followed within minutes.

My thesis is that the assassination disclosure was not a confession that escaped him. It was a **placement** — and the audience was selected for incapacity.

sections.heading: The Provocations Run Cheapest To Most Expensive, Which Is What A Test Looks Like
sections.sourceAnchor: 'You've gotten soft. I insulted you, I barred you, I even mentioned Peach, and you didn't attack once.'
sections.body:
Set the four probes in the order they were used.

**One: importance.** *You're relegated to the B plot.* Cheapest possible provocation, tests vanity.

**Two: access.** The Oracle declines to simply hand over what Bowser wants. Tests patience.

**Three: temptation.** The Astral Shore — a direct route to the thing he came for. Tests greed, and tests whether he reads carefully.

**Four: the dead.** Peach. The one subject in this archive with a documented record of producing arson.

That is not a man losing his temper by degrees. That is an **escalating instrument**, run in the only order that makes the final reading meaningful: establish the baseline with the cheap probes, then apply the expensive one.

And the expensive one is the only probe whose result he actually needed.

sections.heading: The Reading He Took Was Not Trustworthiness. It Was Reach.
sections.sourceAnchor: 'Half the stuff I said I didn't mean. I hope you don't take it to heart.'
sections.body:
Ask what the Oracle *does* with the result, because that reveals what he was measuring.

He does not ask Bowser to keep a secret. He does not swear him to anything. He does not check whether Bowser will repeat it — and Bowser repeated all of it to me within days, which the Oracle must have considered likely.

So he was not testing discretion. He was testing three other things, and all three are properties of an **audience**, not of an ally:

- **Will he attack?** No. Established across four probes.
- **Will he leave?** No. He had already accepted a deadline and needed the tether.
- **Can he check?** No. Bowser was not born in 955 BF. He cannot cross-examine a room that was scrubbed within hours of the killing.

A witness wants to be believed and submits to verification. A **source** wants to be repeated and selects against it. The Oracle picked the one person in the sanctum who was guaranteed to carry the account outward and guaranteed to be unable to test it.

sections.heading: Every Checkable Element Was Already Public. The Uncheckable One Is The Payload.
sections.sourceAnchor: Five or six mages' locks broken. The room untouched. A comb in her hand.
sections.body:
Sort the disclosure by whether the archive could already have supplied it.

**Broken mages' locks** — Guild involvement is the best-documented fact in [the assassination file](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/highsun_1_955_bf_the_day_of).

**Blood on the floor** — [Lady Bloomia](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/lady_bloomia) saw a bloody handprint on the hatch edge that no investigator recorded.

**Guards dying** — the record has guards dead at their posts when Mario arrived, and three witnesses liquidated over the following fortnight.

**She chose it** — the record already says she *chose this death and left evidence for others to find.*

Every one of those is recoverable secondhand by a man who watches. And the one element that is not — **the comb** — is the only detail in the entire account that cannot be checked against anything, because it appears nowhere else in the archive.

That is a peculiar distribution. The verifiable parts are all borrowed. The unverifiable part is the only original.

sections.heading: He Was Wrong About The Only Thing Anybody Could Test
sections.sourceAnchor: 'The guards came in. They all died.'
sections.body:
One claim in the disclosure is checkable, and he failed it.

He said the responding guards all died. The archive says **three guard witnesses alive on Day 1, two dead within two weeks, one vanished.** A fortnight of administrative removal, not a massacre in a bedroom.

In the commentary I first called this *compression* and filed it generously. I withdrew that, and I want to state the reasoning here rather than leave it as a mood.

Compression is what a witness does to a memory. What he produced is what a **reader** does to a casualty list: collapse a sequence of removals into a single event, because the sequence is what you learn from a summary and the event is what you would have seen.

**He got the room right and the fortnight wrong.** That is the wrong way round for someone who was there. The room is the hard part.

sections.heading: What Changes If This Reading Is Right
sections.sourceAnchor: 'I warned her. She ignored me — or maybe she didn't want to listen.'
sections.body:
If the disclosure was placed rather than confessed, three things follow and the archive should hold all three.

**One: the corroborated parts stop being corroboration.** *She chose it* was already canon before he said it. Him agreeing adds nothing and should never have been counted as a second source. I counted it as one for a full pass and I was wrong to.

**Two: 'I warned her' becomes the claim to examine.** His own dossier records him warning about time dilation, warning about the ritual mirror, and warning [Archie](https://mikegent01.github.io/bik/index.html#/article/archie_miser) about absorbing too much power immediately before letting the ritual proceed. The archive already filed that last one as a suspected controlled experiment. *I warned her* is not a new confession. It is his standard discharge of responsibility.

**Three: the comb becomes the whole question.** It is the only thing he supplied that nobody else had. Either it is the detail that proves he stood in that room, or it is the specific invented object a constructed scene needs in order to feel witnessed. There is no third option and the archive cannot currently choose.

analyses.verdict:
**The disclosure should be filed as placed intelligence, not as testimony, and the file should say so on its face.**

The sequencing is the argument. Four escalating probes, then an admission that they were probes, then — to a man just demonstrated to be non-violent, committed, and eighty-five years too young to verify anything — the most emotionally loaded account in the archive. Every verifiable element of it was already recoverable. The single checkable claim is wrong in the direction a reader would get wrong and a witness would not. The single unverifiable element is the only original one.

**This does not make him a liar.** I want that precise, because the archive will want to simplify it. He has never been caught in a falsifiable lie, and the things he said that can be checked are mostly true. That is exactly the profile of a careful source, and careful sources are more useful than honest ones and considerably more dangerous.

**What the archive should do:** stop treating the Oracle's agreement as independent support for anything. Where he corroborates canon, the canon was already there. Where he is alone, he is alone. And the question of whether he stood in that room in 955 BF is now the most consequential open question in the assassination file — because if he did, he is not a custodian who heard about it. He is a party to it.

WAH.

rolls.success: He appears in none of the six. The Day Of record names fourteen people in and around that palace and he is not among them. Either his presence was never recorded, or it was removed, or he was not there — and the archive holds no instrument capable of separating those three.
