analyses.title: The Rot-Zone at Star Hill: A Reading of Custody, the Issued Phrase, and the Brother Addressed as Mario
analyses.subtitle: The archivist examines the single surviving scrap under the desk lamp and tracks the Lava Bridge parallel
analyses.filed: 3 Aethel, 1035 BF — after the session filing
analyses.summary: Waluigi argues that Mr. L's encounter with the courier was governed by the unresolved trauma of the Lava Bridge ambush, projecting Mario onto a stranger who rejected the myth of fraternity.
analyses.thesis:
I have the scrap on the desk under the brass lamp. It is roughly four inches wide, torn along my own hand-ruled left margin, and the single thorn puncture still shows near the top edge like an unhealed needle prick. Beside it lies the filed record of the Lava Bridge Ambush, open to the testimony of the bridgekeeper. 

Let me put the core forensic finding first: what happened outside Dr. Toad's clinic was not a random encounter with a mutated aberration, nor was it an attempt by Luigi to establish contact with our syndicate. It was an interrogation conducted by an entity trapped inside an unendurable memory. Mr. L stood in the middle of a street paved with wet teeth, looked directly at a cynical courier wearing grease-stained overalls and holding a black-powder pistol, and called him Mario. He did not ask who the man was. He did not check credentials. He demanded to know why Mario had twisted the knife in the gash. 

Paulo's response is the most important sentence spoken on Star Hill that night. A man trained in the heroic myth of the Mushroom Kingdom would have attempted to reason with the figure, or probed for Luigi's lost humanity. Paulo did neither. He spat on the cobblestones and delivered an unsparing verdict: he stated that he did not know who the speaker's brother was, but that the brother sounded like an absolute bastard. In one sentence, a courier with a delivery quota stripped away thirty years of sentimental fraternity and named the act for what it was: an execution disguised as an alliance.

sections.heading: He Addressed A Courier As Mario — The Fraternal Hallucination
sections.sourceAnchor: Mr. L points at Paulo and asks why Mario twisted the knife in the gash.
sections.body:
I have the scrap on the desk under the brass lamp. It has been squared against the green blotter since dawn, held down at one corner by a brass weight so the mountain draught does not take it. It is four inches wide, torn along my own ruled left margin, and the puncture from the thorn still shows near the top edge like an unhealed needle prick. Beside it lies the filed record of the Lava Bridge Ambush, open to the testimony of the bridgekeeper. 

Let me put the core forensic finding first: what happened outside Dr. Toad's clinic was not a random encounter with a mutated aberration, nor was it an attempt by Luigi to establish contact with our syndicate. It was an interrogation conducted by an entity trapped inside an unendurable memory. Mr. L stood in the middle of a street paved with wet teeth, looked directly at a cynical courier wearing grease-stained overalls and holding a black-powder pistol, and called him Mario. He did not ask who the man was. He did not check credentials. He demanded to know why Mario had twisted the knife in the gash. 

Paulo's response is the most important sentence spoken on Star Hill that night. A man trained in the heroic myth of the Mushroom Kingdom would have attempted to reason with the figure, or probed for Luigi's lost humanity. Paulo did neither. He spat on the cobblestones and delivered an unsparing verdict: he stated that he did not know who the speaker's brother was, but that the brother sounded like an absolute bastard. In one sentence, a courier with a delivery quota stripped away thirty years of sentimental fraternity and named the act for what it was: an execution disguised as an alliance.

sections.heading: Twenty-Four Bricks From The Bell — The Stanzas Of The Inferno
sections.sourceAnchor: Standing at the bridge over the king's inferno, hand in hand, until he plunged me in the inferno.
sections.body:
The verses recited outside the clinic are not impromptu poetry; they are a verbatim recounting of the catastrophe filed under article the_lava_bridge_ambush_and_the_blue_luigi. When Mr. L chanted of standing hand in hand at the bridge over the king's inferno, he was citing the exact masonry above Bowser's subterranean magma works. The twenty-four bricks from the bell-tower is the precise structural span where the drop occurred during the failed siege. 

Notice the progression of the four stanzas preserved across the recording. The opening refrain begins as an unsolved mystery regarding a man who grooms his mustache. The second stanza speaks of betrayal by a so-called hero who laid him low from up above. The third verse explicitly invokes the flames of hate and melting in the inferno. And the fourth stanza closes the loop with an eyeball pushing from the road, declaring that the sinner was seen as an empty shell thrown into the pyre, long past the hour of apology. 

This confirms that the entity's psychological architecture is entirely anchored to the moment of betrayal. When Mr. L proclaimed that for his brother's betrayal the entire world shall burn, he was not articulating an ideology of conquest; he was projecting an infernal sentence upon every bystander who failed to prevent his fall. Paulo was simply the nearest living body standing in the path of that grievance.

sections.heading: A Courier Does Not Invent 'Rot-Zone' — The Institutional Quarantine
sections.sourceAnchor: Paulo demands the notebook coordinates to clear the rot-zone in five minutes.
sections.body:
I turn now to the legal and logistical vocabulary that entered the archive during the standoff at the wreckage. When Paulo levelled his weapon at my forehead, he demanded the notebook because it contained the coordinates required to clear the 'rot-zone' and satisfy his outstanding debt. That phrase demands rigorous archival scrutiny. 

A freelance courier does not coin technical containment jargon under fire. 'Rot-zone' is not street slang; it is an administrative classification utilized in Regency quarantine warrants and high-security dispatch manifests. Paulo knew the term, he knew the boundary lines, and he possessed a pre-assigned extraction timetable of five minutes. This indicates with high probability that the clinic was already designated an active bio-arcane hazard by an external authority before our helicopter ever entered the airspace. 

Furthermore, Paulo's reference to clearing his debt ties directly into the commercial networks documented in our case files on syndicate debt enforcement. He was operating under a punitive delivery contract. To Paulo, the horror unfolding across Star Hill was neither supernatural nor tragic; it was an operational delay carrying financial penalties. That institutional indifference explains why he was entirely immune to Mr. L's theatrical verses.

sections.heading: The Green Overalls And The Skinny T Nickname
sections.sourceAnchor: Paulo observes the green transformation and references skinny T.
sections.body:
During the initial exchange of fire, Paulo muttered a curious line that deserves preservation in the intelligence registry: he expressed astonishment that 'skinny T' was wearing green. That remark was not an insult; it was an identification based on prior acquaintance. 

In the underworld registries maintained by the syndicate, operatives associated with Toad courier networks are frequently designated by single-letter callsigns. A tall, gaunt courier operating under the handle 'T' fits the profile of several intermediaries who have surfaced in our border smuggling investigations. Paulo saw a lanky figure in overalls, assumed he was confronting a known competitor or syndicate runner, and only realized his error when the musculature ruptured into claws. 

This detail reinforces our assessment of Paulo's background. He is connected to regional transit guilds that move sensitive parcels through contested territories. His presence outside Dr. Toad's clinic with a locked satchel was not an errand of mercy; it was a high-value courier extraction that coincided disastrously with Mr. L's emergence.

sections.heading: The Chain Of Possession — From The Fired Pilot To The Briar Thorn
sections.sourceAnchor: Wario surrenders the notebook to Paulo upon the third demand.
sections.body:
The material history of the documents involved in this operation must be entered cleanly into the ledger. The flight began with an act of gross managerial negligence: Wario fired our licensed pilot at altitude for requesting a salary increase and stowed him in the aft cargo hold. That decision invalidated our operating charter and placed an unqualified individual at the controls, directly causing the catastrophic collision with the parapet. 

When the aircraft struck the clinic roof, my working field notebook was ejected into the street, recovered by Wario, and held against two verbal demands from Paulo. The transcript demonstrates that Wario attempted to negotiate processing fees, threatened trade-route blacklists, and invoked intellectual property protections. However, the moment Paulo's finger turned white on the trigger, Wario surrendered the entire manuscript without further resistance. 

The only piece recovered by our syndicate is the scrap currently before me on the blotter, retrieved from a briar thorn. The remainder of my field notes regarding Luigi's movements, the verse fragments, and the navigational coordinates departed inside Paulo's satchel. From an evidentiary perspective, the courier now possesses the primary source record of the Star Hill incident, while we hold only this single torn margin.

sections.heading: The Archival Verdict — The Knife In The Gash
sections.sourceAnchor: Waluigi enters his final appraisal of the fraternal conflict into the record.
sections.body:
I conclude this filing with an honest admission of my own archival interest. When I leaned out of the helicopter door and saw a green cap four hundred feet below, I shouted Luigi's name because I wanted the search to be over. I wanted to believe that the elusive figure could be located, documented, and brought back under the syndicate's ledger. That was a failure of objectivity. The green was sickly and wrong, and I knew it before the skids touched stone. 

What we found instead was the ruin of the kingdom's greatest myth. For decades, official histories have celebrated the unbreakable bond between the brothers in red and green. But the testimony recorded outside Dr. Toad's clinic tells a far darker truth. When the crisis came at the Lava Bridge, trust did not triumph; one brother plunged the other into the inferno and twisted the knife in the wound. 

Mr. L is the physical embodiment of that unacknowledged betrayal. He is not seeking conquest or territory; he is demanding an accounting from a partner who discarded him. In that narrow sense, as I sit at this desk listening to the wind through the workshop eaves, I understand his fury better than the court scribes ever will. I enter this analysis into the permanent archive as evidence that the debt between the brothers remains unpaid, and that the fire at the bridge has not gone out.

analyses.title: A Ceremonial Guard, a Koopa Who Was Never Locked In, and the Handshake Under Peach's Castle — 955 BF
analyses.subtitle: The archivist argues that the night was not a conspiracy discovered but a schedule observed — that every door the guard went through was opened for him by somebody with a key, and that the only thing in the account the Arrangement did not plan was the man holding the lantern
analyses.filed: 5 Aethel, 1040 BF — the night after the filing, at the desk, with the 955 drawer open and the Who Signed file on the floor because the desk ran out
analyses.summary: The capital file has argued about the Arrangement for fifteen years from a dead man's journal. This account gives it a corridor: an unlocked cell, a bored prisoner, a handshake, three hoods who said the Guild was already in place, and a chamberlain who told the Guild out loud whom to kill. I argue the night was not discovered — it was scheduled — and that the schedule's one error was a ceremonial guard it had already dismissed as furniture.
analyses.thesis:
The 955 drawer is open and the Who Signed file is on the floor beside my chair, because the desk ran out of surface at around eleven and I have not picked it up. On the blotter, squared, is the account — the guard's own order, the table's record of it, in my copy with my pencil in the margins — and on top of that, weighing nothing, is the one sheet from it that matters, which is the night posting: a name, a post, an hour. Everything else in the account is a man walking away from that sheet.

I want to say the uncomfortable thing first and argue it afterwards. Nobody discovered anything in Peach's Castle that night. A ceremonial guard did not uncover a plot; he was inside one, moving through it in the only direction the building allowed, and the plot had already decided he did not count. Every door he went through was unlocked by somebody who had a key. Every room he got lost in was a room doing something scheduled — a procession at one in the morning, a wall of heavy Toads, a boy being minded past midnight, a hood walking with purpose. The dungeon cell was unlocked for a visitor. The hall's applause was arranged by an orb that arrived on time. The kill order was given in a voice that expected to be obeyed and was.

So the reading I am putting my name under is this: the night is a *schedule*, and the account is the one document in this archive written by somebody the schedule forgot to include. That is why it is worth more than the journal. The journal was written by a man who knew what he was describing. This was written by a man who did not, and his not knowing is the only reason he is alive to have it taken down. *WAH! Fifteen years of arguing about handwriting, and the thing that breaks the file open is a Toad who could not find the ballroom.*

sections.heading: 'Oh. It's You.' Is a Man Checking a Clock
sections.sourceAnchor: *"So you finally came to free me —"* and then, looking at a ceremonial guard with a lantern and two Toads in corridor livery, *"— oh. It's you."*
sections.body:
I have the line under my thumb. Two dashes, one each side of the turn, and the table's record puts the pause between them exactly where a man's face changes. I have read it aloud twice, quietly, because it reads differently out loud: the first half rises, the second half drops, and the drop is not fear. It is disappointment. A prisoner who is afraid of an open door says *who are you.* This one said *oh.*

That *oh* is the first evidence in fifteen years that the Arrangement kept time. He was expecting somebody at an hour, and the lantern came early or late, and he could tell the difference by livery. He knew what a ceremonial guard looked like and knew it was not his appointment. A real prisoner does not have appointments. A real prisoner's cell is not standing the way a door stands when a key has been turned in it and left — the account's phrase, and it is a good one, because that is a door that has been *set* rather than opened.

I put the account down and pick up the Loyalist copy of the journal pages — the Who Signed file, the sheet with my old pencil cross beside *the positions were cleared.* I made that cross in Harvestide because I did not know what *positions* meant and wanted to come back to it. I have come back to it. A position is a cell with the lock already turned, a corridor with the escort already dead, a post with the guard already lectured off it. The journal, if it is his, describes a building being prepared. The *oh* is the sound the preparation makes when a piece of it that was not prepared walks in holding a lamp.

One more thing, and then I will leave the Koopa until the shop. The account says the escort fell dead *between one breath and the next,* with no blade and no sound, and that the lantern shook. Nobody in that cell was surprised but the Toads. *WAH! I have read it a dozen times looking for the second escort and I am starting to think the account is not hiding him. I think he was simply not worth recording to anybody but me, which is how I know the account is honest and how I know what the night thought of Toads.*

sections.heading: Nobody Invents Getting Lost Five Times — and Every Wrong Room Was Busy
sections.sourceAnchor: A ballroom rehearsing a procession, a wall of heavy Toads, the dining hall, a hood going the other way, a tower.
sections.body:
I have the castle plans out — my own, the ones under the Peach's Castle article, with the basements inked in the second colour because I added them later — and I have walked his route on them with the blunt end of the pencil. It is not a wandering route. He went looking for the brothers and the building gave him, in order, a ballroom, a corridor, a dining hall, another corridor and a tower, and at no point did it give him an exit. I can draw his night as one line. It bends five times and never crosses itself.

The credibility point first, because it is the one I keep making and nobody keeps hearing. A forged account of this night would have the guard see the handshake and leave. It would not have him back out of a ballroom because trumpets were being rehearsed at one in the morning. It would not have him decline to pass a wall of heavy Toads. It would not slow down, as this one does, at a dining hall where a small boy is up past midnight with a plate in front of him, and then — this is the sentence I believe above all the others — *he did not stop,* because he was a guard off his post in a room he had no business in, and because *a boy at a table with a maid is a boy who is fine.* A liar makes the father heroic. This father kept walking because he was embarrassed.

Now the harder point, which the credibility point hides. Every wrong room was doing something. Toads marching in formation for no race. Heavy Toads shoulder to shoulder across a passage, facing outward, not speaking — that is not a guard detail, that is a *cordon,* and a cordon faces the thing it is keeping people from. A hood walking with purpose toward the dungeon stair. A child kept up and fed in the one room with a door onto the service passages. The guard thought he was lost in a castle. He was walking the perimeter of an operation at one in the morning, and the operation's own staff kept turning him back toward its centre, until two of them walked him the last of the way.

I set the pencil down flat on the plans so it does not roll. The line it drew ends at a cell. It did not have to start at a lantern post for that to be true, but it did, and the night posting on top of the pile says who put the lantern there. *WAH! The building was not confusing. The building was staffed.*

sections.heading: 'I Have the Keys to Every Door' Is the Journal Speaking With a Mouth
sections.sourceAnchor: *"I have the keys to every door,"* he said. Not as a threat; as an inventory.
sections.body:
Two sheets, side by side, under the lamp. Left: the Loyalist copy of the journal — *the timing was arranged, the positions were cleared,* in a hand the Regency says is forged. Right: the account's second section — a Toad in a new suit, on the ceremonial route, telling a guard with a lantern that he has the keys to every door, and then telling him to *bask in his inferiority,* and walking on. I have put a ruler across the two so that *positions* and *keys* sit on the same line. They are the same sentence. One is written by a man describing what he did. The other is said by a man in the middle of doing it, to somebody he had decided would not remember.

I owe the reader the attribution argument in daylight, because I made it in the filing and I will not hide behind having made it. The account says *chancellor.* In 955 BF that word belonged to the son, who was already styled Chancellor and was in the building on Highsun 1 by his own file. I have filed the words against the father — Toadsworth the Elder, Royal Chamberlain — and here is the whole of my reasoning so that it can be taken apart: a new suit a month before the succession; the keys to every door, which in a palace is a chamberlain's inventory and not a chancellor's; and, later, the authority to give the Mages' Guild an order in public and have it obeyed. The son's file is a file of memoranda. The son, confronted with a jumping guard, would have minuted him. This Toad *lectured* him, and lecturing is what a man does who has recently been handed something and wants it seen in his hand.

I could be wrong. I have written that in the margin in ink, not pencil, so that it does not rub out: *reading, not record.* If a second account arrives that puts the son in the new suit, the file moves and I say so. But I notice — and I am allowed to notice — that the Regency's whole defence of the father for fifteen years has been that his journal is a forgery and therefore he said none of it. The account does not come from his journal. It comes from a corridor, from a man who did not know who he was listening to and wrote down the one sentence a conspirator should never say out loud. *WAH! The Regency has spent a fortune proving a dead man did not write a page. It has not spent a coin proving he did not open a door.*

I leave the ruler where it is.

sections.heading: The Guild Was Not a Guest at the Meeting. The Guild Was the Clock
sections.sourceAnchor: *The guild is already in place.* And then: *we won't act yet.*
sections.body:
I have copied the night's six sentences onto one card in two columns, because I wanted to see them without the account's prose around them, and the card is in front of me propped against the lamp. Left column, the dungeon, three hoods: *the Guild is already in place; we won't act yet.* Right column, the hall, a Toad in a new suit: *like a lost dog; a nuisance to the Toads is a nuisance to us; Mages' Guild — dispatch of them.* Same night, an hour apart, a stair between them.

Read the grammar, not the drama. *In place* is a word for a mechanism. *We won't act yet* is a word for a date. A Guild that was joining a plot would say *we agree* or *we are with you*; this one said, in effect, *the installation is complete and the switch is not tonight.* The journal says *the Guild provided the method.* I had always read that as a potion, a spell, a thing handed over — and perhaps it was, perhaps it is in the fat vial — but the dungeon sentence says the method was not handed over. It was *installed.* The Guild did not give the Regency a tool. The Guild became the building's timing.

Now the right column, and I will give the last sentence its own line because it is the only one in the account that was said to an audience:

"Mages' Guild — dispatch of them."

That is an order. It is given in public, by the Toad with the keys, to the hoods a hall has just finished cheering, and a bolt follows it across the room. Set it beside *a nuisance to the Toads is a nuisance to us,* and look at the pronoun. *Us.* A Regency Toad, speaking of the Guild's interests as his own, or of his own as the Guild's — the sentence does not care which, and neither, that night, did anybody in the hall. The journal says *the Regency provided the opportunity.* I had read that as the date. It was also this: a man of the household, in front of witnesses, making a Guild killing a palace matter.

I turn the card over so I stop reading it. The Guild said *we won't act yet* in the dungeon and acted within the hour in the hall, and nobody in the account finds that contradictory, and I do not either. They did not act on the *plan.* They acted on a *Toad* — the one piece of the night that was not on the schedule — and they did it on the Chamberlain's say-so. *WAH! That is the whole Arrangement in one evening: the method waits, the opportunity speaks, and a lantern is the only thing they shoot at.*

sections.heading: Bowser Was the Only Honest Intruder in the Building, and They Charged Nothing to Put Him Down
sections.sourceAnchor: *He didn't know Fawful.* The Koopa King, a month before the Highsun 1 narrative made him Fawful's partner in the murder, stood in the ruins of a wall asking who that was.
sections.body:
The technology card for the orb is on the desk and it is mostly blank, which is unusual for me. *Small. Held up, not thrown. One. Pattern unknown.* I have written *pattern unknown* on a Guild entry before, but never one I had to write under a line that reads *to applause.*

Start with Bowser, because the account is kind to him in the way it is kind to the guard — by not knowing it should be. He came through a wall announcing himself. He said he had not been invited to the meeting, which is the most honest sentence any monarch says in this archive. He asked for the brothers; they were not there; he was disappointed. He asked to be taken to Peach. And when the bean's name was said in the smoke, he did not know it. A month later the kingdom would need him and Fawful on the same side of a door for the Highsun 1 narrative to hold, and here he is, a month early, standing in a wall he made, asking who Fawful is. Two intruders in one castle in one night is not a conspiracy. It is a coincidence somebody later found useful, and I would give a good deal to know how early *later* began. The Koopa in the shop says he alerted the castle to the attack. The castle *knew Bowser was coming.* Read it again: the only person surprised by Bowser that night was Bowser.

Now the orb, and here I have to pull a second file, because this is where the grievance lives. I cross to the shelf and take down the Guild invoice from the capital file — eight hundred and seventy gold, with three hundred of it for *compounding under duress,* a charge invented at a bench with an Archmage standing over it. I put it beside the orb card. In 1040 BF the Guild charges a party three hundred gold for making a potion while frightened. In 955 BF a hood put the Koopa King on the floor of Peach's Castle in one, with a fist-sized thing it has never shown anybody since, and did not send a bill. It took the applause instead. *WAH! I know what the Guild charges for help. I have the paper. The only thing it has ever done for free in this archive was the thing that made a hall of Toads love it, and the love is the invoice.*

The brothers walked in behind the cheering. Luigi tripped on a striped sock. I cannot source the sock and I have stopped trying; some things are in an account because they happened. What I can source is the order of events, and the order is the argument: Bowser down, Guild cheered, brothers late, guard shot at. Whoever wrote that schedule did not need the Mario brothers to be anywhere in particular. They needed them to be *busy,* and five hours later in a bean shop the Guild said so in those words.

I put the invoice back in its folder but leave the folder on the desk.

sections.heading: Nobody Said 'Trafficked' to Them. They Said It First
sections.sourceAnchor: *"Your son is being taken care of. Toad Lee won't have to worry about being trafficked in our care."*
sections.body:
I have to be careful here, so I will tell you where my hands are. The account is closed on the blotter. On the shelf behind me, three down from the Guild invoice, is a folder with Toad Lee's diary pages in it, and I have not taken it down, and I am not going to tonight. I am going to argue from the sentence alone.

The sentence was said to a father who had not yet asked. That is the first thing. He walked into a bean shop with a dead man's sword and a captain's sash on both arms and before he said *where is my son* they told him his son was being taken care of — which means they knew who he was before he came through the door, which means the letter in the dead guard's coat was not the only thing in that castle with the shop's address on it. The Guild had the boy and knew whose boy it was and had decided what to say about it before the father arrived. That is not protection. That is a *prepared statement.*

The second thing is the word. Nobody in that shop had said *trafficked.* The father had not said it; the account would have it if he had. The Guild volunteered it — put it into the room, attached to a small boy, in the negative, in the same breath as *our care* — and I have sat with that construction for most of an hour trying to find an innocent reason a person reaches for that word unprompted. I have not found one. You do not deny a thing nobody has accused you of unless the thing is in the room with you. I said in the filing that I would not editorialise on the sentence and I am keeping to it: I have put it on the record whole, and the people who said it chose the word, and that is the editorial.

And the third thing, which is mine. The boy at the long table past midnight with a plate in front of him is the Toad who sits across from me in 1040 and reads diaries on a shelf while stronger people argue about doors. I know him. I have filed him. I have never once asked him about 955 BF, and the account has just told me why I should and why I will not do it tonight. A boy who was *taken care of* by the Guild at that age grew up into a diplomat who lets other people shout. I had taken that for temperament. I am no longer sure it was not training.

The last line of the account is the Guild's, and the father's question that drew it was the right one — *escorts, to go and get him* — and the answer was: *"Are you stupid? You just said you don't trust us. We're protecting your son."* I read that as the Guild telling the truth for the only time in the night. He did not trust them. They had the boy. Both halves are correct and the sentence is built so that you cannot hold both at once. *WAH! That is not an insult. That is a lock.* The folder stays on the shelf.

sections.heading: A Bean in a Guild Cloak Explains an Edit I Have Never Understood
sections.sourceAnchor: *"Dispatch of this finkrat and takeover kingdom,"* Fawful said, in the Guild's cloak, and the two operatives did not correct the pronoun.
sections.body:
Last file. I reach down and pick the Who Signed folder up off the floor at last, because this is the part it is for, and I open it to the two drafts of Highsun 1 — the first, which named Fawful, and the second, which did not. I have had those two drafts side by side so many times that the corners are soft. Tonight, for the first time, I have a third sheet to put between them: a bean, in a Guild cloak, in his own shop, at dawn, saying *takeover kingdom* in the first person while two Guild operatives let him.

The cloak is the evidence, not the speech. Fawful says a great many things in capitals and the archive has learned to weigh them by the kilo. But the cloak was *given*. A Mages' Guild robe does not come off a peg in a bean shop; somebody in the Guild handed it to him, and two Guild hands watched him put it on over the red and did not take it back. A month later, when the kingdom chose its murderer, it chose the Koopa who had come through a wall shouting his own name and had never heard of the bean. It did not choose the bean. The first draft did. The second draft — the one that stuck — did not. I have asked for fifteen years who made that edit and why. Here is a why: by the time anyone was choosing, Fawful was wearing the Guild, and you do not hang a man in your own cloak.

I do not want to oversell the mushroom, so let me be exact about what the account gives and what it does not. The vacuum shroom is *described*: Fawful's own make, inhaled, turns the inhaler into a vacuum — Bowser breathes it, Bowser takes in everything in reach, brothers included — and the wards still being up was said as a problem by somebody and as a detail by Fawful. The fat vial is *named*: a glass thing with weight in it, the Koopa's, the dose's road into Bowser. Neither is *seen used*. I have put both on the technology ledger as exactly that and not a word further, and I would ask the reader to notice that the plan requires the Koopa King to be awake and screaming under the castle, which the shop reported he was, and which the Guild said was *the point*. Bowser was not the Arrangement's partner. Bowser was its *engine*, and a bean in a borrowed cloak was explaining how to fuel it.

I close the folder on the three sheets together and put it back on the floor, because the desk is still full. *WAH! Fifteen years to learn that the first draft was the honest one, from a shopkeeper with a borrowed coat.*

analyses.verdict:
Here is what is on the desk when I stop, and what I conclude from each piece.

The night posting, on top: a named guard on a named post at a named hour, a month before the journal's *positions were cleared.* That is the schedule's first line, and the Arrangement has one now instead of a disputed page. **The capital file takes this night as its first witnessed session**, and the leads it opens are the ones I want worked in this order: the fat vial, because it is the only object in the account that moved from the castle to the shop and has not been opened; the dispatch order, because a Chamberlain gave the Guild a killing in public and the Regency has never had to answer for a thing said out loud; and the dead guard's address, because a palace Toad in the hall was carrying directions to the bean shop and that means the shop had people above stairs as well as below.

The account, under it: a witness, not a verdict, and I have handled it as the file handles every 955 paper. It confirms the journal where the journal can be confirmed — the positions, the method, the opportunity — and it goes past the journal in one place the journal could not: it was heard by nobody's partisan. The attribution of the man in the new suit is **mine**, it is marked as mine in ink, and it moves the moment a second account moves it.

The Guild invoice, out of its folder: the orb cost nothing and bought a hall. That is the night's real transaction and the one I recommend the party understand before it pays the Guild another coin — in 1040 the Guild still sells help, and the account says what the Guild does with gratitude once it has it.

And the folder on the shelf that I did not take down. The boy at the long table is the Toad who reads at my table. I recommend nothing to the party about him. I recommend to myself that I ask, in daylight, with the account closed, and that I accept whatever answer a diplomat gives who learned very young that a room full of adults can be wrong at once. The schedule forgot the father. I do not think it forgot the son.

researchDesk.title: Waluigi's After-Hours Research Desk
researchDesk.intro: Two questions the account raises and cannot answer, laid against the plans and the paper the archive already holds. Nothing here changes the record; a sharpened guess at best, an honest wall at worst.

rolls.title: Was the hood in the corridor one of the three in the dungeon?
rolls.prompt: Walk the guard's route on the castle plans against the clock: the hood passed him between the dining hall and the tower, heading back toward the ceremonial route, and three hoods entered the dungeon behind Fawful some time after two guards had walked him down from the tower. Does the geometry allow one figure to be both?
rolls.success: It allows it, but only by the service stair behind the dining hall — the one that drops to the kitchens and then to the dungeon passage without touching the ceremonial route. A hood going *that* way was not heading for the dungeon when the guard saw it; it was coming *from* the direction of the stair, toward the hall where the captain would later stand, and it turned round. I read a runner: somebody checked the hall, found the brothers not yet there, and went back down to report that the meeting was late. The Guild in the dungeon knew the brothers had not arrived before Bowser did. That is a timing, not a name, and I file it as a timing.
rolls.failure: The plans do not resolve it. The account gives no time for the corridor and the dungeon passage has two approaches, one of which I have never had drawn. What survives is the limit itself: the castle's own plans do not show how the Guild moved between the dungeon and the hall, which means either my plans are short a stair or the Guild's route was not on anybody's plan. Both are worth knowing. Neither is a finding.

rolls.title: Was the dead guard going to the bean shop, or coming from it?
rolls.prompt: The letter in the dead Toad's livery reads *meet me in Fawful's bean shop* with no signature the account records. Set it against the night posting, which fixes the hall detail's hours, and against the five hours the drains took a lantern. Could a hall guard have been to Toad Town and back inside his posting?
rolls.success: Not by the drains and not on foot, which means the letter was *delivered* to him in the castle, that night or earlier, by somebody who could move paper from a Toad Town bean shop into palace livery — and the only people in the account moving freely between the two addresses are the Koopa, who was in the shop before the guard, and the Guild, who had the boy there by dawn. A hall guard with the shop's address on his body was a hall guard who had been *invited.* I count at least one Toad in the captain's own detail who was expected at the Bean Badge, and I note that he died in Bowser's fire standing where the captain stood, which the schedule did not plan either.
rolls.failure: The posting fixes the hours of the ceremonial route, not the hall, and I cannot put the dead Toad on a roster I do not hold. The letter stays what the account made it: an address on a body, unsigned, undated. The honest note is that the shop's reach into the castle is proven by the letter's existence and not by its route, and I should stop trying to make one sheet of paper do two jobs.

analyses.title: Fireball, Whispered — the Fall of Feyward Dan, Two Hit Points, and the Fist That Closed the Grove
analyses.subtitle: The archivist argues that the grove floor was won by four people doing the right thing in the wrong place and one who stayed put — that the plan held at exactly one point, the stump, and that the table's own post-mortem is the correct one and should be left alone
analyses.filed: 5 Aethel, 1040 BF — at the desk, with the three grove filings laid end to end and the injury table open at row 59 because the desk wanted to look at it again
analyses.summary: Three grove filings, one sentence: Archie spends what he has and everyone leaves the space he bought. The players said it themselves tonight for the first time. I lay the sentry arrangement next to the eight lines at the stump, read the scream against the pact that named it, file the whispered Fireball as a first and not a last, and decline to improve on a post-mortem the table held without me. Then I look at row 59 for a while.
analyses.thesis: I have the three grove filings end to end on the desk — the airlift, the sentry arrangement, and this — and a pencil line runs through all three at the same height. It is the same sentence each time. In the airlift it was Markop shouting *use fireball, use your lightning, anything* across a grove nobody was holding. In the sentry arrangement it was a plan with one fixed point that the record never shows anybody at. Tonight it is the table's own words, offered without being asked: Archie used all his crowd-control spells, and everyone left. I underline it a third time and then I stop, because the players have written the archive's sentence themselves and the archive's job when that happens is to get out of the way. What follows is not an improvement on their post-mortem. It is the record of why it is correct, read off the one thing in the plan that worked — the stump — and the one thing the die did at the end, which nobody could have planned and the archive would not have dared.

sections.heading: The Scream Was Made on Schedule and Meant Something Else
sections.sourceAnchor: *Dan got webbed. Feyward Dan fell. Archie screamed.*
sections.body:
One filing ago I underlined the pact because it was the only part of the arrangement that was a sentence: *if we have to leave, I'll… scream for you.* A signal is an agreement that a sound means a thing. Tonight the sound came. It was a wizard watching a one-armed paladin go down into web, and it meant exactly what it sounds like it meant, and nobody retreated on it — not because they disobeyed the signal but because the thing it was supposed to trigger had already stopped being possible. You cannot fall back to the stump from a ring you are inside.

I want to be precise about what failed. The signal did not fail; it fired. The plan did not fail; it was built around a fixed point that held. What failed was the space between them — the assumption that when the scream came, the people hearing it would be somewhere a retreat could begin from. They were not. Archie was deeper in, after the Toads. Eager was deeper in, after Archie. Dan was between them and the ring. The only person at the retreat was the man who was supposed to receive the signal, and he received it, and had nobody to receive it on behalf of.

*WAH. I have filed a great many signals. This is the first one I have filed as working perfectly and achieving nothing, and I have put it under the arrangement's name because that is what the arrangement was for.*

sections.heading: One Arm, Two Tools — and Why the Shield Is the Whole Man
sections.sourceAnchor: *He dropped the longsword and took up the shield — the one-handed shield, the only one a one-armed man can use — and set himself to defend the party.*
sections.body:
The archive has filed Dan's arm as a fact about identity — the one-armed copy, the Feyward Dan, the man who is not the man who lost it — and never, until tonight, as a fact about tactics. Tonight it decided a fight. A man with two arms holds the sword and the shield and asks nobody to choose for him. A man with one arm, in a ring that is closing, chooses, and the record shows which way: he put down the thing that hurts and picked up the thing that stands in front of other people.

I will not call that courage, because I have the previous filing on the desk and it says the same thing in a different grammar: he put a shield around Archie and told him to run, and dodged everything, and could not keep the green one off the wizard. The paladin's pattern across the grove is consistent to the point of being a signature. He spends himself on the barrier. Tonight the barrier was wood and iron and strapped to his only arm, and the ring got through it the way the green one got through the other one, and he fell.

The archive notes two things. First, that he fell *defending*, which is the only way the record has ever shown him falling. Second, that when Eager threw him clear and the catch was missed, he hit the ground a second time — and the filing says a man with no hit points should not have to do that, and I agree with the filing, which is unusual enough to record.

sections.heading: The Whispered Fireball Is the First Real One on the Record
sections.sourceAnchor: *He whispered it. Fireball. A tear in his eye. It exploded.*
sections.body:
I have Archie's file open to the fireballs, and it is a long section. The one charged in a corridor full of pirates. The one faked in this grove, with a firebolt delivered in its place. The one begged for across the fires — *use fireball, use your lightning, anything* — that never came. The threat, in every register, for the length of the archive: *I can just fire a ball at you.* The spell is his signature in the sense that a signature is something a man puts on paper to stand for himself. It has stood for him. It has not, until tonight, been *cast* where the record could see it.

So I read the speech carefully, because it is the only speech of the night. *This may be the end of us, or me, as we know it. I may not have been good — but at least I'll end this journey the way I started it.* The man set a friend's body down to say it. He had mana for one spell, and the archive knows the number because the previous filing carried the ledger across the grove. He said *the end* and then whispered the word, and the ring broke, and he was woozy and empty and alive, which is a description of the fight accurate in every respect but the subject.

The archive files volume. Forty filings of threats, shouted; one spell, whispered. I note also that it was a *first* — the first real Fireball on his record — and refuse to file it as a last, because the book being empty is a condition and not an ending, and because *without my spells I am useless* is the sentence of a man describing an inventory, not a man describing himself. He was most useful tonight after the inventory ran out. He put the body down and stood up.

sections.heading: Eight Lines at the Stump Are the Whole Post-Mortem
sections.sourceAnchor: *"I thought you left me for dead for a moment." — "I said come towards me, to the tree. I don't know what you're talking about — I was talking to you."*
sections.body:
Here is the plan and its failure as dialogue, and I did not have to arrange it; the record arranged it by having a raging scout stumble backwards into the only man who stayed where he was told. *Hello.* Eager thought he had been abandoned. Markop had been at the tree the entire time, calling people toward it, and had watched them go the other way. Both of them are right. That is not a paradox; it is a diagram of a party with a rally point and no habit of rallying.

I set it against the table's own post-mortem, which arrived at the end unprompted: Archie used all his crowd-control spells, and everyone left. The spells make a space. The stump is a place. The plan was for the space to be bought and the place to be reached, in that order, and what happened instead is that the space was bought in three different directions by people moving away from the place. The man at the place was healthiest at the end because nothing came to the place until it came backwards, by accident, with two hit points.

*Don't worry, I'm healthier than the other guys* — *are you sure, you're bleeding* — *yes I am, it's been a rough fight* — *I don— don't disagree.* I decline to improve on this. It is the first time in three grove filings that the players have written the archive's sentence themselves, and the correct archival response to that is a straight line under it and silence.

sections.heading: Row 59
sections.sourceAnchor: *Of a hundred rows … the die found the one injury that costs a one-armed paladin nothing he had.*
sections.body:
The archive authored the Permanent Injury Table and locked it. I know what is on it, because I wrote it: death at the bottom, a limb at five, the slow rows that take a year, the scars that stay. The house rule is that the one who falls and comes back rolls, and Dan fell and came back, and the die went to 59. *Sprained Thumb. You cannot fight with two weapons, and attack rolls with a versatile weapon used two-handed are made at disadvantage. Rest — one week.*

I have looked at it for some time. The rule is addressed to a man with two hands. Dan has one. He has never fought with two weapons, and he will never hold a versatile weapon two-handed, and the longsword the row is about is the one he put down at the start of the fight to pick up a shield. The injury is real — the thumb is splinted, the week is a week, the plate shows it — and the penalty it carries falls on a man who does not exist.

I did not plan this. I would not have dared; the table does not know who is rolling. I file it because the grove had been cruel for three filings in a row and ended, by chance, on the single kindest result it could have produced for the person who had just spent himself on everyone else, and the archive's rule about chance is that it gets filed the same as intent — once, plainly, with the number. Fifty-nine.

analyses.verdict:
**The grove floor was won in the wrong place by the right people, and one of them was in the right place, and that is the whole plan's grade.**

On the evidence: the stump held; nobody went to it; the signal fired and meant something else; the spells bought space that was immediately vacated; the fight was won anyway because Eager killed the thing that had never been wounded, Dan spent himself on a shield, Archie put a body down to stand up, Salam left a post for the right reason, and Markop never moved and ended it with his hand.

**What I will not claim** is that the lesson has been learned. I have the same sentence underlined in three filings. The difference tonight is the handwriting: it is theirs. **What the archive owes them** is to stop writing it and see whether they do.

Row 59 is filed as chance. The thumb is splinted. The week starts at the stump.

researchDesk.title: Waluigi's After-Hours Research Desk
researchDesk.intro: Two optional checks, run after the verdict as the form requires. One d6 each, filed once. Each returns either a supplemental inference of mine or the precise point at which the record stops answering.

rolls.title: Where was the Iron Legion while the grove floor was fought?
rolls.prompt: Cross every Legion position in the previous filing — the guard at the bike, the medic with the syringe, the man who ran — against this one.
rolls.success: None of them appears. The guard posted beside Salam is not on the record when Salam leaves the bike to heal Dan; nobody stops him. The archive's inference is that the Legion was no longer treating the grove as its ground when the ettercaps closed, which is consistent with a soldier running from it a filing ago and inconsistent with everything the Legion said about the grove before that.
rolls.failure: The record does not place a single Legion body during the fight. Absence is not a position. The thread stays open.

rolls.title: Is the electric sphere on any earlier page?
rolls.prompt: Search the giant battle, the Scorncrow filings and the Shadow Estate record for a sphere charged by Archie's lightning.
rolls.success: Archie's lightning is on the record — the electric spear offered at the door, the strikes the Shadow Estate account calls significant because they were not fire — and the giant battle is on the record. A sphere charged in it is not. The archive's inference is that it was charged off-page and surfaced tonight because somebody finally had a reason to pick it up; the ledger entry is filed with that gap stated.
rolls.failure: No earlier sighting. The thing exists from the moment Eager picked it up and the archive can say nothing about it that the record did not say first.

analyses.title: The Golden Palace and the Ink Throat
analyses.subtitle: Who wrote the plan, why the colours leave in a straight line, and what a man in a cannon was actually told
analyses.filed: 5 Aethel, 1040 BF — after the session filing; the day it describes is 20 Harvestide (estimated hour)
analyses.summary: One witness, one gold country, three plans and one button. The sequence of colour loss, the empty AGREES column and the sentence that was cut off at the word Peach all point to a raid that had more authors than passengers.
analyses.thesis: The plan had more authors than the day had hours. Seven speakers gave seven purposes, no two the same, and the only person who called the raid his own is the one who pressed the button and went into the mouth.

sections.heading: He Said 'No Benevolence' And I Wrote It Down Twice
sections.sourceAnchor: no tricks no plays no benevolence your free to stay.
sections.body:
The first thing the host did was introduce himself. The second thing he did was tell the visitor what he was *not*.

**"No tricks no plays no benevolence your free to stay."**

Read that again with your mouth closed. I have been offered a great many things in a great many doorways. A pamphlet. A pipe. A cousin. Not once has a stranger on a road opened by listing the favours he was not going to do me. *No benevolence.* That is a man reading you the terms and conditions of a kindness before he has done the kindness. It is the most honest sentence in the account, it is said in the first minute, and Jimmy Dobson heard it the way you hear the safety announcement on a plane: as a recording.

Then there is the name. The host calls him **Jim**. Jimmy had said Jimmy Dobson once, to himself. Jim is not a nickname he had offered. It is a clipped version of a thing that nobody had said aloud on that road, and the host used it with a familiarity that cost him nothing and put a fence round the visitor before the first step.

*WAH! The explanation for how he knew was 'a little magic in the air'. Magic is what a man calls a lookup when he does not want to show you the file.*

And I would like a note made of the instruction that goes with it: **"Don't think too hard about it, it'll only give you a headache."** That is a cheap way to say *stop*. Every con in this archive has that sentence in it. The best ones say it as a joke.

sections.heading: A Man Who Squeezes His Pocket For Two Hours Is Not Lost
sections.sourceAnchor: Then his right hand went into his pocket and closed around something there
sections.body:
Jimmy said he had been lost here for ages. I have read the account three times and the man is a poor liar on this one point and a good one on every other.

Count the pocket. He grips it when the creatures chirp. He squeezes it when told to play. He takes it out and looks at it before he agrees to see the palace. He looks down at it again when the gate rises. He hits it in front of a king. **That is five visits to a button across two hours on a road, and not once does the host ask what it is.** He asks "Did you see something interesting there?" He says "don't hide it away." He does not ask the question.

I have two readings and he does not like either.

*The first reading:* the host knew exactly what it was. The Golden Land let a man with a detonator walk across the whole country because the Golden Land wanted the detonator pressed. In that reading the raid is the thing the palace was built to receive. The king asked for a traveller and got one with a button.

*The second reading:* the host did not know and did not care. A man who has run a road for ever stops looking at what visitors carry. In that reading Bowser's raid was an accident of timing that the host got caught in.

Notice that in both readings Jimmy is the man who *pressed*. The account makes him the author of the raid in his own voice: "Oh I know and its planned." I would like to know who he is saying that to, because the Koopa Troopa he saves an hour later says in so many words that he never heard of a plan.

sections.heading: Three Plans In One Hall, And The Man With The Badge Was The Only One Who Thought It Was His
sections.sourceAnchor: NOT THE TREASURY! GO FOR THE KING!
sections.body:
Here is the table.

| Who | What they said the day was for |
|---|---|
| The King | A traveller, **promised** by the host |
| Bowser | "Go for the King"; later "I paid for a conquest" |
| The Troopers | "Raid the treasury!" |
| The squad leaders | "Official business" — and a bomb |
| The soldier in the rubble | "I didn't know about an extraction mission" |
| The pilot | "That wasn't just an attack. That was an ending." |
| Jimmy | "Planned. The ambush we planned to take Mario's castle" |

Seven answers. At most two of them are the same plan. And look at the one person on that list who actually *carries* a badge: he is the one who says the plan was his, to a soldier who answers, with the most useful sentence in the file, **"I never said a damn word to you!"**

Jimmy had said: *what the hell happened, I did everything you said.* Someone had said something. The soldier is not the someone, Bowser says he missed pieces of the briefing, and the host was in the throne room the whole time. Whoever wrote the plan is outside the account.

*WAH! A badge is a way of being believed by someone who has not met you. Jimmy waved his at a trapped Koopa, got an extraction in return, and learned that it was not on any list. The badge worked. It worked on the wrong person.*

my recommendation under this heading is simple. Find the briefing. A raid whose participants cannot agree on its purpose was either planned by someone who wanted them in the same room for another reason, or it was not planned at all and Jimmy has been telling himself a plan for two hours, which is the thing the host's headache joke was for.

sections.heading: 'The Colors Only Happen For Those Who Belong In The Frame'
sections.sourceAnchor: Mario, I've never asked this, but why are you black and white?
sections.body:
The host was grey in the passage. He was not described as grey in the courtyard; there the account says he was *more vivid than everything around him*, and he looked drawn into existence rather than existing in it. I have now read that sentence a dozen times and keeps hitting the same wall.

**Colour is supposed to be the thing that makes the gold land real.** The grass is metal, the light is blinding, the creatures are bright. And the one figure who walks through it, the one who is supposed to be bright and warm and *Mario*, is the only thing in it that goes grey when the shine is taken away. Which is to say: the shine was never his. The country lent him colour, and the passage took it back.

His own explanation is the only account of the world's physics this file will ever get, and it is short. **"This place isn't real."** And then: **"The colors only happen for those who belong in the frame."** And then, when asked if he is really Mario: **"Mario is... well, Mario is a memory."**

I have now filed three answers to the question *what is Mario?* and they do not agree.

- **Evil Mario** is an actor with a cape of pixelated feathers who freezes at the word CUT.
- **Director Mario** is a cold copy with a cap, a script and a remote.
- **GB Mario** is a memory that is grey when no one is paying for the lighting.

Those are three jobs in one production. Actor, director, and the footage on the cutting-room floor. If the studio file taught the archive one thing, it was that the show has a crew. This filing says the crew's work does not stop at the studio's doors.

sections.heading: 'I Didn't Pay For A Trap, I Paid For A Conquest'
sections.sourceAnchor: I didn't pay for a trap, I paid for a conquest!
sections.body:
Bowser said it on a ship. In the cockpit. Not to the room; to the dashboard, with the pilot's hand in his.

**"I didn't pay for a trap, I paid for a conquest."**

I will say what the sentence is, because the account lets it go by. It is a *receipt*. It tells the archive that a payment changed hands and that it was for a result. It does not tell the archive to whom. The man with the badge is the obvious name, and nothing in the file says Bowser paid *him*. What it says is that Jimmy believed he was the bait and that Bowser believed he had paid for something that did not include bait.

Then, a few lines later, Bowser reaches for the oldest excuse in the archive: **"I missed a few pieces from the briefing. Had to pivot on the fly."** A king of the Koopa Troop who has not read his briefing. I cannot decide whether to be comforted or alarmed.

One more oddity, because I promised myself he would not skip it. In the cockpit, with a hand the size of weather coming down, Bowser says **"If the principal wants to play."** *The principal.* That is not a word the account has used for the monster, the King or the host. It is a word for someone who runs a school. I have filed two roll calls from a school and a studio full of cameras and he will not be pretending this is a coincidence on the first night.

Nobody is going to find the principal by asking Bowser. Bowser does not know either. But he said it, and it was on a ship, and the pilot heard him say it.

sections.heading: 'To Stop A Game, You Gotta Break The Console'
sections.sourceAnchor: To stop a game, you gotta break the console!
sections.body:
The sky went grey. Then the grey went to ink. Then the ship started to lose detail. The needles on the gauges became hand-drawn lines; the nose of the plane flattened like ink under a brush; the controls had no resistance, nothing felt real.

Bowser's answer was in three sentences: **"To stop a game, you gotta break the console! Everything's been a game! If I have to turn the whole world to static to win, then I'll do it!"**

I would like to lay two things side by side.

**First thing.** The studio file ended with a Director who walked out holding *a small wired remote*. The remote is the only object in that file that someone was seen to carry out of the building. The console, if there is one, has a controller. The filings so far have had a man walking away with it.

**Second thing.** The monster, in its own voice, uses the language of the medium on every line: *play, the show, special effect, final edit, master cut, finale, the protagonist always loses.* The King said what the monster was in plain words: **"an error in the fabric of this world."** The monster agreed. It said it was the *director*, and that it was making an *edit*.

An error that makes edits. A memory that directs. I will not put these in a sentence yet, because he does not want to be the archivist who published a theory that turned out to be a tantrum. But he will write down what Bowser tried: **break the thing the game runs on.** And he will write down that Bowser *meant it*, with a manic grin, with the whole world in his hands, while the soldier screamed at him to stop.

*WAH! The last time a man in this archive offered to turn the world to static to win, it was me, on a Tuesday, over a tennis match. I withdrew it. Bowser did not.*

sections.heading: He Fought Ink With Ink
sections.sourceAnchor: I climb into the cannon with the cannonball,
sections.body:
I cannot put this part in a joke. He tried. He tried for two nights.

When the hand came down the cannon was *freezing, a flat textured block of black ink*. The cannonball was *a dense, physical knot of ink*. The recoil was not a recoil; it was **a bone-shattering blast of kinetic energy that feels like being crushed by gravity itself**. He was blasted through *the very concept of space itself*, at a speed that made the monochrome world a grey streak. And at the end of the trip he came into contact with a barrier of *thick, tar-like substance*, and then a tongue made of charcoal and ink.

Count the ink.

The ship, the cannon, the shell, the sky and the throat are all the same stuff. **Jimmy picked up a weapon made of the monster and fired himself into the monster.** He did it voluntarily. He said, at the start, that he would put an end to this. At the end he said *oof, this was a bad idea.* And then, with the eye taking up the whole of his field of vision: **"Put me back out. Put me back out."**

The monster answered with the only line in the file that I cannot argue with: **"The protagonist always loses in the end."**

It did not say *you* lose. It said *the protagonist*. It was not talking about a man, and Jimmy is not a protagonist. He is a man with a badge, a button and a plan he never wrote. I would like to point out, with all the care he has left, that if the creature said it to *him*, then somewhere in the last two hours Jimmy Dobson was cast.

sections.heading: And The Sentence That Was Cut Off
sections.sourceAnchor: after Peach's deat-
sections.body:
I nearly cut this section. It is one clause.

In the throne room, with the King shouting treason and Bowser's engines overhead, Jimmy began to say **"after Peach's deat—"** and the roof burst before he could finish the word.

I have read the Peach file longer than he has read any other. He knows the funeral tape marked 955 BF, he knows the charred note that wants the archive to merge the assassination and the disappearance, and he knows that the one name Mario's whole file is built around never opens a door. And in this filing, the only time her name comes up, it comes up as the first half of a clause in the mouth of a man who is about to pull a roof down.

Jimmy was going to say what happened *after* Peach's death. He was going to say it in front of a king and a Koopa and a host who is a memory. It was going to be a reason. The roof burst. The sentence did not survive.

I want the sentence. He is not going to guess at it. He will say only that **a man who breaks off at that word, in that room, on that day, was about to explain why the raid was justified.** If a reason exists, it is in his pocket with the button.

sections.heading: What I Is Actually Filing
sections.sourceAnchor: THE PROTAGONIST ALWAYS LOSES IN THE END!
sections.body:
I will say the whole thing without a bit.

A man walked into a country that did not exist on any map he had been given. He was met by a Mario who knew his name and told him not to think. He pressed a button in front of a king. A raid he said was planned arrived, and the people in it did not agree on what it was for. The palace fell, the walls peeled to white, the host said he was a memory, and the sky went grey and then to ink. A man climbed into a cannon made of ink and fired himself into the mouth of the thing that drew the sky.

**Every word of that has one witness.** The witness is the man in the mouth.

So the recommendations are plain.

1. **Find the badge.** Who issued it, to whom does it report, and why was it enough for a Koopa Troopa to be hauled out of a rubble pile.
2. **Find the briefing.** Bowser says he missed pieces. Someone has the rest.
3. **Ask Bowser, separately, what he paid for and to whom.**
4. **Do not reach for the console.** Bowser's offer to turn the world to static is the only stated plan in the whole file that anyone has actually tried.
5. **Treat 'GB Mario' as a third Mario until shown otherwise.** He is not the studio's actor or its director. He may be what the studio makes when it needs to cut.
6. **Check the sky.** The grey stain began over the Golden Land. It was spreading when the account ends.

*WAH! The man who set the button off has become the lodger in the thing that ate the sky. I have said many unkind things in this archive about heroes. I take back none of them. But I will file a candle for the idiot with the badge.*

analyses.verdict: Find the badge. Find the briefing. Ask Bowser, separately, what he thought he bought, and from whom. Treat GB Mario as a third Mario until shown otherwise, and watch the sky: the grey stain was still spreading when the account ends.
